Name: Arthur Huan
Question: During the events of Fallout New Vegas, Mr House claims that he could get humans into space to find a new unharmed planet, do you believe this was simply House lying to get you to join him or could he have actually done it?
Answer: I believe he is genuine, but genuinely mistaken and misguided. Alternatively, he is genuine and correct, but more evil than perceived. Let’s get one thing out of the way first: Mr. House’s overall space faring dreams are well within the realm of reason. The difficulty is not in getting to space or reaching other planets. In New Vegas, we see REPCONN, a company that specializes in producing rockets, and a subsidiary of RobCo, Mr. House’s company. Walking through their HQ, we see their promise of broadening humanity’s reach to the stars. Scattered around the Mojave, we see old REPCONN assets, including the rockets that the Bright Brotherhood took. In Fallout 4, we also see mention of a battle in the Sea of Tranquility, meaning battles were fought on the moon. The technology is very close. I have complete confidence that Mr. House, with his mind set on this goal, and all the resources at his disposal (if the Courier cooperates and secures a House victory), would be able to perfect pre-war tech and continue research, allowing manned ships to other planets. But what then? There aren’t any habitable planets within a reasonable distance. Mr. House wasn’t talking about mining resources or sending scientific probes, he specifically mentioned “colony ships”. I don’t think the Fallout universe is anywhere close to achieving even close to light speed travel, let alone the sci-fi methods of faster-than-light travel that enables people to colonize other habitable planets. This means Mr. House is probably setting his eyes on nearby planets, like Mars. (For convenience, I’ll just treat Mars as the target planet. Anything I say will also apply to any other candidate.) For Mars to be habitable, we would need to terraform it. This is surprisingly viable. Fallout has cold fusion, G.E.C.K.s, and possibly other technologies that will help us terraform. If they don’t exist, they might be researched and invented. Even with just what we know, the Fallout universe already has a huge leg up on the real world. The trouble lies in the scale, though. Smaller settlements are quite doable, but if you want most humans to be able to leave Earth, you’ll need to entirely transform Mars, and in particular give it an atmosphere. That is a tall task, and I don’t see how it will be accomplished. In this, I say Mr. House must be mistaken and misguided. He either doesn’t understand that there’s no habitable planet in proximity to Earth, or underestimates how much has to be terraformed. However, likely he is not so naive. We will now try to unmask Mr. House and get at his real intentions. For starters, let’s pose a very simple and natural question: Why not terraform Earth instead? Fallout doesn’t have overpopulation, there are too few humans. Fallout isn’t that irradiated, especially when compared to Mars. Fallout has the best clean energy in fusion. Why does Mr. House decide to undertake a project that’s hundreds of times harder, instead of just terraforming the Earth? If he really thinks he can be the best leader for humanity, an autocrat ushering everyone into a new era, shouldn’t he go with the simplest, least risky, and most profitable option? That of simply terraforming the land that’s already beneath our feet? Is it pure sentimentalism and idealism? Is Mr. House not the rational businessman he claims to be? Or, does he want to make Mars the new Strip and Earth the new Freeside? Think about it. Realistically, within a few centuries, we’ll at best establish some dome settlements on Mars. But, without an atmosphere, it will be inconsequential for humanity at large. Yet, for Mr. House himself, this would be invaluable. He will be completely secure on another planet, putting the vacuum of space between him and his enemies. He will have a monopoly on space travel—there will be no NCR monorail, only REPCONN space shuttles. Finally, he could even hang a sword over everyone’s heads, in the form of orbital laser platforms. His old rival, Poseidon Energy, had already shown us the possibilities. Beam fired by ARCHIMEDES II And none of this has to be sinister. In his own mind, he will be the noble one. Mr. House sees himself as humanity’s best. In doing this, he will be doing humanity a service, both by keeping their great leader alive and safe, and by providing humanity a backup world. (Even if, realistically, only humanity’s wealthiest and most influential could visit that world.) This is a chilling future, and perhaps too big a leap to make. Yet, this is the only possibility I can think of, that aligns with his character and explains his goals. It is, in some sense, merely an upscaled version of what he already positioned himself to be. Hopefully, I am wrong. If not, then we can only pray that Courier Six is still in his good graces when his plans come to fruition, and will be one of the lucky few that get to join him. (Of course, killing him is also a great alternative.)

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Are there any bad endings in Fallout: New Vegas?
Answer: Absolutely there are! In fact, every ending is a bad ending. That’s part of what makes New Vegas such an enduring game, that none of the endings are definitively good. You are only picking among the lesser of the… four… evils. Different people value different things, which explains why there are still discussions to this day about which faction is the best or the worst. Among the four, I feel that Yes Man and Caesar’s Legion are the worst endings. Going with Mr. House or the NCR still leaves the Mojave in a bad state, but at least we see more positives. I am even somewhat on the fence about whether the NCR ending could legitimately be considered a good ending. Yes Man A lot of people thought that an Independent New Vegas under the Courier and Yes Man is the best ending, potentially the only good ending. I was among these people. Unfortunately, the more about the lore I know, the worse this ending seems to get. Let’s get the obvious things out of the way first. Yes Man is basically Skynet, commanding an army of killer robots. Worse, unlike Skynet, he is effective impossible to kill. You can’t just send a missile to where the AI is housed. You’ll need to actually kill all the securitrons. It’s also quite likely that he is, like Agent Smith from The Matrix, a program that the system has lost control of and cannot be erased. Otherwise, Mr. House, sensing his presence, would’ve dealt with him already. Now, even if we suppose Yes Man will always be good, will never be taken advantage of by an evil master, won’t be corrupted or hacked, the condition of New Vegas is still terrible. Independent New Vegas isn’t actually a Courier-led New Vegas. It is an anarchistic society, with Yes Man and the Courier providing security against outside threats with their securitron army. This doesn’t solve any of the glaring internal issues, and one of the negative consequences is the fall of the Followers of the Apocalypse. You’ll find that if you choose this path, no matter how much you help them, they will still eventually be overrun and fall, leaving the Mojave worse off without their knowledge, aid, and medical assistance. Descending into anarchy is a terrible idea, especially when your society was already a chaotic shithole. Throw in an unkillable Skynet and his killer robot army, and you have just paved a road to hell through good intentions. Caesar’s Legion Caesar modeled the Legion after the Roman Empire, except that he didn’t understand Rome at all. Rome built infrastructure and offered its citizens a lot of privileges/rights. They also weren’t as cruel and bloodthirsty as popularly portrayed. If anything, the NCR is more like Rome, especially considering the NCR’s biggest taint being that it forces people to integrate and become its citizens, exactly what Rome did. I have a ton to say on why the Legion is a bad idea on every single level. However, I’ll hold off on that and simply say, a society where: …is atrocious and horrible. If not for Yes Man, it is the worst ending in New Vegas, hands down. If you go with one of the two other endings, namely Mr. House or the NCR, then there are a lot more positives, but I still see enough issues to classify them as bad endings. I appreciate this game design, though. There’s simply not a perfect faction available in such a situation, and we have to make do with what we are given.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Before 2005, did any members of the audience believe that Darth Vader's injuries were faked in order to gain the sympathy of Empire supporters?
Answer: I’m sure there are. There are people who believe that the moon is made of Swiss cheese and that rats’ favorite food is Swiss cheese. However, there is a mountain of evidence to show that Vader was heavily injured, and zero evidence that they were faked. So, I can bet that over 99% of the audience didn’t believe in this kind of conspiracy theory. I also can’t think of anything to justify why the Empire’s symbol of terror, meant to inspire fear and crush enemies both psychologically and physically, should be sympathetic. Ever since he first appeared on-screen in ANH, Vader was shown to strike fear into everyone around him. It was only ever built upon in later movies. This definitely translated for the audience, as it’s a major reason that Vader was such a beloved and iconic villain. We are spoon-fed information about how the Empire wishes to inspire fear and rule that way. We are shown how Vader and the Empire at large is perceived, time and time again. There’s no reason to believe the Empire would attempt to portray Vader as a tragic figure deserving of sympathy. EDIT: If anything, such a conspiracy theory has more basis after the Prequels came out. Not that Obi-Wan didn’t chop off Vader’s limbs and leave him to burn on Mustafar, but that maybe Palpatine purposefully wanted Vader to be injured to garner support and sympathy. It could be similar to his famous “the attempt on my life has left me scarred and deformed”. He could say, look at how the Jedi turned on their own, the few good heroes who stayed loyal to the Republic. Look at how cruel and horrific they are, and how necessary Order 66 was. Even so, there’s no evidence for this, so it’s still merely a conspiracy theory.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: If Darth Vader can use the force through his cybernetic arm, why can't he use Force Lightning?
Answer: Force lightning isn’t some overpowered combat technique that every Sith should learn. It’s not necessarily more powerful than many other Force powers. What makes Force lightning special is its capacity to torture. (Which is why it’s exclusive to the dark side.) Even if you’re using it to kill, you’re killing in a way that inflicts pain and suffering. It’s kind of like crucifying someone instead of just decapitating them. If there’s one thing I know about torture, though, it’s that there are many methods to achieve similar results. Vader had his own preferred methods, ones where he doesn’t risk frying himself and all his robotic components. If he truly wanted to use Force lightning, I’m sure he could. And he did, in an illusion. In fact, his lightning was red, the most potent and rare kind. In the real world for Vader, however, I struggle to imagine a scenario where he would need to electrocute someone. He could probably achieve the same or better results by choking, crushing, pushing, or hurling heavy objects at an opponent. And these won’t require electrocuting himself to perform.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: What is the significance of Obi-Wan's flirtatious behavior with Asajj Ventress in "Star Wars: The Clone Wars"?
Answer: There is absolutely zero significance. Well, apart from potentially racking up attention or excitement in some people, which evidently worked judging from this question. To understand why Obi-Wan seemingly flirted with Ventress, we need to first understand who Ventress is as a person, and then conduct a multi-layered analysis of her psychology, and then cross-reference encounters that she has with others. This will give us a picture of her modus operandi. After we conclude the analysis, we can then continue on to examine Obi-Wan’s actions. We can likely assume that having dealt with her before, Obi-Wan would undoubtably understand Asajj’s habits and mindset, and we can operate under this assumption to extract the potential reasons for him behaving in such a way. Or, we could do the easier thing and just let Obi-Wan explain it to us. In Dark Disciples, Obi-Wan explains to Quilan Vos: Come now Vos, you can't tell me you managed to go undercover in all sorts of shady places without flirting yourself. With Ventress, it's a power play, a way for her to exert control. It will serve you best if you engage in it with her. Also, I recommend rewatching the scenes. You’ll notice that it’s actually Ventress initiating and doing the harassing, flirting, and, dare I say, assaulting. Obi-Wan was merely playing along. He might have seemed to be having a little more fun than expected, but he is Obi-Wan. It’s hardly out of the ordinary for him to be witty and playful.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: How powerful is Han Solo's blaster compared to the stormtrooper blaster?
Answer: Han uses a modified DL-44 blaster pistol. The stormtroopers used the E-11 medium blaster rifle. You can probably already see that this is somewhat of an unfair comparison. We are comparing a pistol to a rifle. The saving grace, however, might be that the E-11 is a medium blaster, and Han has one of the most powerful blaster pistols in the galaxy. Still, a pistol is a pistol, and a rifle is a rifle. At longer ranges, it’s not even up for debate. Han’s blaster does not compare to the E-11 in power. A DL-44 pistol only has an effective range of up to 75 meters, while the E-11 can effectively shoot targets at up to 300 meters. At closer ranges, the pistol does its job admirably. Blaster resistant stormtrooper armor is never a problem. Still, E-11s also shoot straight through stormtrooper armor. This is pretty reminiscent of real-world firearms. No matter how good your body armor is, at closer ranges, even pistol rounds can penetrate. Being at a closer range trumps everything. It’s not proof that Han’s pistol is extraordinarily powerful. I can’t seem to find any extraordinary evidence, so for now we can safely assume that there is no extraordinary claim to be made. It’s definitely possible that Han’s pistol surpasses some light rifles, or lighter configurations of rifles. But, to match the power of a proper rifle, you’d want the rifle configuration of the DL-44. In the pistol configuration, it is a good weapon, giving you ample firepower and good accuracy, but it’s still just a pistol.

Question: What is the order to watch all the Star Wars? Is it still called the Machete order? Why was the order called that? Has it changed?
Answer: There’s no definitive order, it’s all subjective. The Machete Order itself was never a consensus, just another way to watch the movies. It’s called the Machete Order because it first appeared in a blog called “Absolutely No Machete Juggling”. The blogger named the order after himself. In his own words: “I’ve dubbed this ‘Machete Order’ on the off chance it catches on because I’m a vain asshole.” I believe you can still find it on here: To summarize, the blogger doesn’t believe we should follow either the Release Order (OT into Prequels) or the Episode Order (Prequels into OT). The Release Order suffers from you not being able to fully grasp how Anakin’s story went, and how important the final moments in RotJ are. And the Episode Order, well, spoils a lot of the things for you in the OT (Original Trilogy). The machete order is basically to: He gave many more justifications, check out the blog if you want to see more. The addition of stories like Solo, Rogue One, and the Sequels haven’t, as far as I know, changed the order. If you are convinced by the reasoning, then this could be the order for you. You can watch all the others after finishing the five movies. Personally, I’m still a proponent of Release Order. It doesn’t matter that watching the Prequels will change your perspective on the resolution in Return of the Jedi. I’d argue it’s better, in fact, because you will be able to experience it twice. It’s rare that you are able to experience a great ending to a story twice. I also don’t think the spoilers matter that much for Episode Order. With meme culture and so much internet exposure, for such old media, pretty much everyone and their dog knows the most important beats, like “No, I am your father.”

Question: If the clones did not have inhibitor chips, would they have executed Order 66 or would they refuse and remain loyal to the Jedi?
Answer: Yes. Most of them would have, anyway. There was a time before inhibitor chips were introduced as a concept, when the Prequels first came out. They were a very recent addition to canon, the first appearance in 2014, and not widely known by the general fandom until years later. We might’ve all come to accept them, but for over a decade they were not required to justify Order 66. Imagine you are a clone commander. Literally your entire life, right from birth, you’ve been indoctrinated to be fiercely loyal to the Republic, at a complete disregard for your life. You are human, yet are trained to be as close to a droid in loyalty and obedience as possible. And you are proud of this. Your loyalty is a virtue. There is an order from the highest authority that a highly capable and dangerous individual, your Jedi general, is a traitor to the Republic and must be apprehended/executed immediately. Do you do it? Heck, in the real world, commanders for nuclear launch subs are expected to carry out an order from their head of state, effectively killing possibly hundreds of thousands of people at the press of a button. And they have much more humanity in them and are allowed much more individual agency. The clones aren’t allowed to ever disobey illegitimate orders, like real-world military commanders are. On top of that, also consider that most Jedi were not like Obi-Wan, Anakin, or Plo Koon. Most Jedi generals were more akin to Pong Krell. Why do you think people took a liking to Plo Koon for his actions and words here? It’s because he was rare. The vast majority of Jedi did see the clones as completely expendable. As a clone, you would’ve seen countless of your brethren needlessly wasted, and not any remorse from the Jedi. I don’t care how good of a person you are, if your superior treats you coldly and doesn’t give two shits about you, and you are expected to sacrifice your life for them, you will come to hate them. Now, couple that cold indifference with a complete incompetence and stupid errors. (Remember, Jedi aren’t trained as military commanders, they are the farthest thing from qualified.) Are you absolutely certain that your Jedi commander isn’t another Pong Krell? Are you sure that they’re not sending clones out there to die uselessly, on purpose? I suspect some clone commanders were itching to kill their Jedi generals before Order 66 even came down. In conclusion, the inhibitor chips were not a necessity for Order 66 to have been carried out by the clones. However, I do think it is a good addition to the story. It makes the Jedi’s demise more complete and assured. It also allows you to tell some fantastic stories of Jedi treating their clones in the right way, but still be turned on at the drop of a hat, like we saw in the Clone Wars series.

Question: If the world's strongest Chess engine were constrained by not being able to actually capture any of the opponent's pieces, but could still give check and checkmate, how weak would the opponent need to be to lose?
Answer: Anyone, and I do mean anyone, who understands the rules of chess, will easily win against this engine. Including a 3-year-old toddler. You can get your king castled by move 4: Congratulations. You are now invincible. The only piece that can check your king is a knight. It is the only piece that can “jump” over pieces, all the others will be blocked off. And since they can’t capture, you have a permanent blockade. However, you’ll notice that the only squares that a knight can check from, in this position, are e2, f3, and h3. Two of these squares are occupied, and the last one is guarded. You can even occupy it, and now your opponent won’t even be able to give a check, let alone checkmate you. In fact, this idea isn’t unique to this setup. Let’s say you had your king castled queen-side instead. You’ll notice, once again, that there’s no way to give more than one check. Simply put, if the king is on the last rank, there will be at most 4 squares that a knight can check it from. It would be trivial to surround your king with pieces, and occupy or defend these 4 squares. The knight won’t be able to get in, and all the other pieces are blocked off since they can’t capture, so your pieces are a blockade. Now, you’re defensively invincible. What about offense? Just get your queen out and capture everything. Your opponent cannot take back, so basically every single piece is hanging.

Question: Besides Palpatine, who would've been a better choice for Episode Nine?
Answer: Rey. I feel like she might be the only choice, in some sense. Imagine you are J.J. Abrams. You need to come up with the main villain for the last episode of a trilogy. After The Force Awakens, you had Kylo Ren set up to be the new Vader, Hux to be the new Tarkin, and Snoke to be the new Palpatine. You even had some fans speculating about Plagueis connections and a variety of other things. There were plenty of options. Then, this happened. So, the big bad is gone, and Hux is now a lesser villain. You only have Kylo left. Unfortunately, he’s always been a whiny little bitch, and was never popular enough to be the main antagonist. In the OT, you had Vader, the most iconic Star Wars character, and there was still a bigger villain that was the endgame. Kylo is not going to be able to compete. Who, then? You cannot introduce a new character. It would be suicide to set up a new character as your main antagonist, in the movie that wraps up a trilogy. Nor would it be ideal to bring back a character from previous media. It has to be a major character that has appeared in the trilogy already. So, here’s what I propose. A solution that makes the most out of the limited resources in characters that we can play with after The Last Jedi. We must pull another Anakin and make Rey a main villain by the sequel’s end. It wouldn’t be original, but at least there’s potential for a good story. Here’s my vision for what the storyline would be. Be warned, I haven’t put a lot of thought into this, and came up with this on the spot for the answer. Without proper guidance, after coaxing and manipulation from Snoke and Kylo, Rey has been inching towards the dark side. After being told her parents are nobodies who sold her for drinking money, Rey’s entire world crumbles. It’s the last straw, and for the first time in the movies, she displays real flaws and turns to the dark side. This has been set up and hinted towards already, so it wouldn’t be a hard road to go down. Rey the dark sider joins forces with Kylo Ren, who is now the Supreme Leader, just like in the current version of Episode IX. They form a force dyad, just like Revan and Bastila Shan, so now they would fully embrace it and achieve more than they could before. Plus, none of the Resistance knows about Rey’s turn to the dark side. She decides to utilize this. The rest of the movie will build suspense as we follow Kylo and Rey making preparations to deal the final blow to the Resistance, on one side. On the other side, we give characters like Poe and Finn some screen time, and flesh out their characters and stories. We can even have Finn learn lightsaber combat from someone, and start awakening his Force abilities (something I will fully give to him in this version). It will go something like Sabine receiving training from Kanan and Ahsoka, but make sure to not make Finn too powerful. The most he should be able to do is akin to Luke’s lightsaber pull in the Wampa cave, if not even less. Finally, in the climax, Rey approaches the Resistance fleet in her ship. She boards, and the slaughtering starts. We can draw inspiration from Vader killing the Separatist leaders in RoTS, Vader killing the Rebels in Rogue One and ANH, Baylan and Shin working their way through the New Republic ship in Ahasoka, and Luke’s scene in the Mandalorian. I think I would especially enjoy that Mandalorian scene, where everyone in the bridge of the ship watches the camera footage in horror as the Force user mows down everything in their path. Rey kills everyone, except Poe, who had already escaped in his X-Wing, and Finn, who briefly duels her with the lightsaber, and distracts her to escape. As this is happening, we can cut to scenes of First Order fleets arriving at important worlds. We can see scenes of walkers firing on military bases, TIEs and capital ships blowing up local fleets, stormtroopers blasting their way through an urban area and setting everything ablaze, and politicians being shot or detained and taken away. The galaxy had fallen into the hands of another authoritarian regime. Finally, at the end of the movie, this scene explains the title. Rey is there to hunt down Poe/Finn, when the encounter happens. It can go exactly like the current version. The prequels ended with the return of the Sith, and the sequels will end with the rise of the dark sider, who would also hijack the Skywalker legacy. [P.S.] We might even have some stories set hundreds of years in the future, where we hear about how the Skywalkers are remembered by the people. There’s Anakin Skywalker, the monster born out of the Force, who gave rise to this bloodline of the galaxy’s biggest villains. The youngling slayer and oppressive dark lord of the Sith who helped enforce Imperial oppression. There’s Luke Skywalker, the false prophet who formed a false Jedi Temple, to lure in and murder Force sensitives, including his own nephew Ben Solo. Some conspiracies even suggest maybe Ben was his own son, born from his famous incestuous past with his sister. After that, there’s Rey Skywalker, Luke’s prized apprentice and daughter, the treacherous agent hidden in the Resistance, who destroyed it from within, and then went on to co-rule the galaxy with an iron fist alongside Kylo Ren. This is irrelevant to the answer above, but I think it’s an interesting idea on how history can get twisted, so I wanted to share it nonetheless.

Question: You are suddenly placed in charge of the Republic Navy (Star Wars) in the Clone Wars era. How would you fix its many problems?
Answer: Let us first evaluate the state of the Republic Navy and what strengths and weaknesses it has. The obvious place to start is the mainline capital ships in the Venators. The more I see of them, the more impressed I am. Their successors, the ISDs, might be more massive and imposing, but few capital ships in Star Wars beats the elegant practicality of the Venator. They had an insane carrying capacity for smaller ships, from starfighters and interceptors to bombers and troop transports. In fact, the entire central red line on the Venator are hanger doors. They can be opened to reveal the half-kilometer flight deck below, allowing quick and simultaneous deployment of starfighters. Therefore, even though the Lucrehulk carriers used by the CIS might have more carrying capacity, I’d still prefer the Venator as a carrier, because they can deploy starfighters faster and over a larger area. (Thrawn can attest to the issues with deploying all your starfighters from a specific opening.) Of course, this is not without drawbacks. The flight deck and hanger doors are a structural weakness. Furthermore, Venators were great at carrying, but lacked firepower. Maybe you could complement them with other large ships that were more focused on a powerful armament, but the Republic didn’t do this. This leads into my first, and most major, improvement: I would add more ship variety. I would complement the Venators with some ships with heavier firepower. A prime candidate could be the Victory-I class Star Destroyers. (The actual predecessors to the ISDs, if I may say so.) Like the later Imperial Star Destroyers, they had a much more powerful armament, with 12 quadruple turbolaser batteries and 40 double turbolasers, compared to the Venators’ measly 8 turbolasers. (The Venators did have better point defense and proton torpedoes, but these are hardly enough.) If every fleet had a 1:3 or even 1:2 ratio of Victory to Venator Star Destroyers, we would have a lot more options and flexibility. Now, in every battle, there is real pressure on the enemy capital ships from our guns. Such a fleet composition might even force the Lucrehulks to have to stay even further back to avoid the more powerful turbolasers, and thus reducing the stress on our starfighters. (Droid fighters had to stay within a certain range of their carriers.) Besides, these are smaller and cheaper to produce than Venators, so it would help the economy and logistics, too. I think this is the most important change to be made.

Question: Would it have been possible in 1999 for Liam Neeson to play Mace Windu and Samuel L. Jackson to play Qui-Gon Jinn without making the Star Wars Prequels inconsistent with the Original Trilogy?
Answer: It would not make the slightest difference. Mace Windu and Qui-Gon were completely new characters. The Prequels could not contradict the Original Trilogy no matter what it did, as long as we end with Palpatine as the Emperor, Vader as his Sith apprentice, Obi-Wan and Luke with the Lars on Tatooine, and Leia on Alderaan. That is all that mattered. We could have had Anakin grow up in the Jedi Temple completely unproblematically, and then be mind-controlled by Palpatine with a chip implanted in his brain, causing him to kill everyone. Obi-Wan might have taken Anakin’s DNA to Kamino secretly to make Luke and Leia. Anakin and Obi-Wan could have been lovers, before it turns out Obi-Wan was actually a female changeling, and that’s how Luke and Leia came to be. It would make the Original Trilogy very weird to watch, but nothing inconsistent here. Vader could have been a space dragon with a polka dot dress, having just laid two beautiful eggs, before Palpatine decided to turn her into a human male. And then Obi-Wan would, with some help from a holocron, turn the two baby dragons hatched from the eggs into Luke and Leia. Horrific writing? Yes. Inconsistencies with the OT? Nope. I could go on, but I think you get the idea. Even if Qui-Gon and Mace Windu just never existed, it wouldn’t have caused any issues.

Question: What are the top 100 most powerful entities in Star Wars Legends?
Answer: There’s a blatant AI answer on this question. Besides, Quora is flooded with AI-generated answers anyway. I think it could be fun to see what ChatGPT says. Spoiler alert: it is horrific. Question: Is it arguable that Obi-Wan Kenobi is the best Jedi ever? Not most skilled or powerful by far, but the best Jedi?
Answer: I wholeheartedly believe that when talking about the “best” Jedi, we shouldn’t be talking about who is the most powerful. That would be like saying the best Shaolin monk is the best at martial arts, or the best military commander must be the best swordsman, or the best detective must be the best marksman. Heck, even if the job description is mostly to shoot people, like for a soldier, there are far more important things than marksmanship, like teamwork, trustworthiness, toughness, etc. Jedi are sci-fi warrior monks, meaning they should be judged on how good they are as a monk first and foremost. Yoda was the best swordsman in the Jedi Order, but that is a happy coincidence. His position as Grand Master is primarily based on his wisdom and knowledge of the Force, and his embodiment of what it means to be a Jedi, not on how well he can fight (it does also help, of course). Now, while Yoda is probably the best person to be a mentor and leader for Jedi, I think Obi-Wan is arguably the best person to embody what it means to be a Jedi. He was a better Jedi than Yoda. There, I said it. There are many aspects to this, but here I want to focus on one thing: his devotion to the Jedi way despite all he’s gone through. He witnessed Darth Maul kill Qui-Gon. Holding his dying master in his arms, he promised to mentor Anakin, even despite the inadequacy he must have felt. And he took on that responsibility well, becoming a wise, patient, and understanding mentor. He also switched from Ataru to Soresu, becoming more defensive-minded. This is perfect in reflecting the Jedi mindset of not aggressing. During the Clone Wars, he was re-united with his former love interest. At this point, we should note that Obi-Wan fell for Satine when he was 15, even younger than Anakin when he had his emotional struggles. Ultimately, though, Obi-Wan overcame his human nature and didn’t give in to his urges. Satine died in his arms. He might not love her anymore, but he certainly cared deeply. Why does everyone keep dying? Well, at least he could focus on mentoring Anakin, who was growing into a great lad. Unlucky. Obi-Wan had trained up the greatest Jedi slayer ever. He had to digest this knowledge along with the knowledge that most of the Jedi had been wiped out in an instant. Literally, the entire world has collapsed. The Jedi are destroyed. So many of his colleagues and friends are dead. The Sith have won and are in control of the Republic, which likely won’t last much longer. There’s no time to even recover from this shock, however. He has to now confront and kill his figurative brother. He controlled himself and rose to the occasion. He could’ve been crushed, but wasn’t. Even though he won, he lost everything at that moment. He deserves this meme way more than Thanos ever did: Why does everyone keep dying? Soon after, Obi-Wan was once again taking on responsibility for the hope of the galaxy. To Obi-Wan, Anakin proved himself not to be the Chosen One, and even if he initially didn’t think Luke was the Chosen One, he and Leia were next to the only hope they had left. He did struggle and was pathetic for many years on Tatooine. But, that is only natural. Are we expecting a 40-year-old who suddenly lost everything, with the seeming entire world on his shoulder, to have everything figured out? He fared better than Yoda, to say the least. And Yoda was supposed to be the wisest and strongest (mentally) Jedi, with almost a millennium of life to aid him. Yoda went to Degobah to waste away his waning years. It was Obi-Wan who held onto hope and kept trying. It was Obi-Wan who kept on trying to convince Yoda to train Luke/Leia before the latter gave in. This alone was enough to convince me that Obi-Wan was the best Jedi, not Yoda or anyone else. Let’s also not forget that Obi-Wan had to live with his failure and mistake in not killing off Vader by his own hands, possibly dooming the galaxy. Obi-Wan, the near-perfect Jedi he was, did eventually find peace. That is but a taste of why Obi-Wan is, in my humble opinion, the best Jedi. He went through hell and never for a moment deviated from his devotion to the Jedi, the Force, and to democracy.

Question: Why don’t any Star Wars ships have wheels? They either walking legs or they fly. Did they never invent wheels?
Answer: There are both wheels and treads in Star Wars. Admittedly, they are a bit rarer, for reasons I’ll discuss later on. Case in point, the Separatists’ Persuader-class droids: Their Hailfire droids: The Occupier tank used by the Imperial occupiers: (The tank had both a repulsorlift version and a treaded version.) And the Juggernaut, used by the Republic and later the Empire: Why aren’t they used more commonly? To start off this discussion, I think an evident point is that armor with repulsorlift technology, AKA hover tanks, have an obvious advantage over wheels, treads, and walker legs. You don’t have to contact the ground, so bumpy terrain and smaller obstacles are all not a problem. However, the fact that they don’t contact the ground can also be a detriment. We know many shields wouldn’t allow hover tanks through. Ideally, you would then need to have something that is grounded to walk through these shields, if possible. So, now the question is just down to wheeled vehicles (or treads) versus the walkers. I think part of the answer is in the name of the AT-AT, AT-ST, and AT-TE. The AT in their names stand for “All Terrain”. And that’s the first piece of the puzzle: having long legs allow you to traverse more kinds of terrain. We can walk over a pothole and through snow and mud, even if our cars might get stuck. (Treads somewhat help, but in muddy terrain, or when the highs and lows are too extreme, they still would get stuck.) Another reason is, especially with the AT-AT, elevation is a tactical advantage. Being able to see much farther and fire above everything is very useful. Even with lower walkers like the AT-TE, they’re still higher than most wheeled vehicles, unless you use gigantic wheels like on the Juggernaut. Last but not least, the most important reason: They look cool.

Question: In Avatar, was Azula more powerful than Ozai? If so, why didn't she try to take over the Fire Nation from him?
Answer: Nope. Ozai was the most powerful firebender (by far) before Aang took away his powers. This is usually the case—Fire Lords are typically the most powerful firebender as well. (As for why that’s the case, that’s another discussion.) Even if Azula is more powerful, even considering how much fire nation culture values power, power is not everything. Or rather, raw physical power is not everything. You also need political power and other types of power. Imagine if Azula initiated an Agni Kai, challenging for the throne, and won. By law, Azula would then become the Fire Lord. But what would happen then? She will be seen as the daughter who usurped her father, who was a great Fire Lord in the eyes of most. More than a few eyebrows will be raised, and some generals and officials might outright defy her and back Ozai. Even if initially, people listened to her and respected her new position as Fire Lord, Azula would be a terrible ruler. She knows very little about politics or keeping people willingly loyal. Look at how well she retained her “friends”, even when they were unburdened by power struggles and other complicated affairs. Azula might be able to gaslight and threaten her subjects into compliance, but that won’t be a permanent solution. Emotions and grudges will fester. Considering that she would have usurped the throne in the first place, I suspect disgruntled generals and officials won’t have much trouble coming up with an excuse to dispose of her. And the people, who largely loved and even worshiped Ozai, would cheer when her inevitable downfall occurs. Of course, all of this would be different if Ozai willingly passed on the position. But, if Azula were to try to take the position by force, not only would she be humiliated in the fight, but also she won’t keep the throne for long if she did win. Azula likely knows this. She might be arrogant, but she’s not stupid.

Question: Besides Palpatine & Darth Vader, which ancient or modern Sith Lords has the potential to become the most iconic character of all time?
Answer: I have two candidates in mind. The first is Darth Bane. The Rule of Two is one of, if not the most iconic feature about the Sith religion as we know it today. Yoda’s line, “Always two, there are. No more. No less. A Master and an apprentice.”, even highlights its in-universe significance. As a result, the Sith Lord who came up with it, while neither the most powerful nor the most interesting, is among the most famous by association. There’s hardly a Star Wars discussion about the Sith, that won’t mention Darth Bane and his Rule of Two. There are many fascinating Sith Lords from Legends. For instance, the Sith Triumvirate, consisting of: Nihilus, who is a literal wound in the Force and could suck stuff. Revan, though, is almost like a main character that many of these characters revolve around, both on the Jedi and Sith sides. Darth Malak was Revan’s apprentice, and his greatest moment was arguably his betrayal of Revan. Finally, my favorite. Bastila Shan’s story with Revan is just absolute gold. I usually hate romance stories, but this one is one I’m fond of. Plus, their descendants were a glorious bunch, with many standouts that helped change history. Revan himself is also quite interesting. While many other Sith Lords had their own quirks and unique specialties, Revan does, too, despite the seeming plainness at first glance. For starters, his dual lightsabers are absolutely badass, and arguably the most recognizable lightsaber(s) in Star Wars, at least among oldheads. Kylo Ren’s lightsaber might be more recognizable nowadays. His aforementioned involvement with so many characters and momentous events is another point. His journeys between the light and dark sides as the story progressed, is also quite something. One discussion about this was what introduced me to the character in the first place. There are many other great things about Revan. I will stop reminiscing, and let you be the judge of whether or not he deserves this spot. I think he does.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Is it possible to build a life-size Jedi Temple from Star Wars in real life?
Answer: No. We wouldn’t even be able to get the base foundation in, let alone the Jedi Temple itself. When you look at this picture of Coruscant, you aren’t actually looking at a bunch of buildings on the ground. You are merely looking at the highest level. Ground level, the layer of Coruscant built on the actual ground of the planet, is so far below the surface structures, that few people even know much about it and what goes on there. There are over 5000 such levels. We can’t even build a building with close to that many levels, let alone structures that cover the entire surface of a planet. (Coruscant is roughly the same size as Earth, so this is a fair comparison). For comparison, the Burj Khalifa is the tallest building in the world, at a height of 828 meters (830 to the tip). It also as the most floors, at a “measly” total of 163 floors. So, just the basement levels below the Jedi Temple, would be an impossible undertaking for us to build. Okay, we won’t be able to build all the layers below the Jedi Temple, but about part of the Jedi Temple that’s above the surface? I mean, it looks quite small, right? When I first saw it, I imagined it as around the size of maybe Westminster Palace, at most. And boy, was I wrong. I think you can excuse my naivety. For one, I was a literal child back then. For two, most skyscrapers and our tallest buildings look like this: Thin buildings with an average base area, just really, really tall. Well, the Jedi Temple is really, really, really tall. It stands at around 1 km, or 1000 meters. The aforementioned Burj Khalifa is only 828 meters tall. And unlike these tall buildings humanity has been able to build, the Jedi temple is not a thin structure. Its base structure is absolutely massive. Simply eyeballing it, the base length and width is more than its 1 km height at least. That would make it almost 200 meters taller than the Burj Khalifa, while being 16 times larger at the base. Of course, the Jedi temple isn’t a solid cuboid, the towers at the top are much smaller. But, even taking that into consideration, what we’d basically need is to build ten copies of The Pentagon next to each other, and expand it upwards at least 20~30 times, if not more. For reference, the Pentagon is the world’s second-largest office building, with 6.5 million square feet of total floor space. The world’s largest, the Surat Diamond Bourse, has 7.1 million feet of floor space. The Jedi Temple would have 10 million feet of square feet, at least, in a single floor. The Jedi temple would be the world’s largest office building by far if it was only 4 meters high. But no, it’s roughly 500+ meters high, with 500 more meters of multiple towers above that. The scale is truly unimaginable. In conclusion, it would be impossible to build even the 5000+ levels of under what we see of the Jedi Temple below the surface. And the surface portion, would make the Jedi Temple the tallest and largest building on Earth, by many orders of magnitudes. Theoretically, it is possible. Realistically, it’s impossible. NOTE: In Legends, the Imperial Palace, which was basically the refurbished Jedi Temple, was said to be 500 meters wide at the base. This makes no sense, because at every angle, the Jedi Temple looks wider at the base than it is tall. At only 500 meters wide, the Jedi temple would only be twice as wide at the bottom than most skyscrapers. It doesn’t look like a fatter skyscraper, so this is almost certainly wildly inaccurate.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Was there anything the Jedi Order could have done to save themselves and the Republic once the Clone Wars had already began?
Answer: If the Jedi Order was omniscient, and knew what we as the audience knew, there might have been a way. The Separatists were so powerful, that they posed an existential crisis to the Republic. In order for the Republic to possibly survive, you needed both the clone army and Palpatine. The former are the troops fighting and resisting the Separatist armies, and the latter is holding everything together politically, as well as a huge symbol for civilian morale. This meant that, even though the Jedi were highly suspicious of the clone army and rather unsettled at the political maneuvers of Palps, they couldn’t do anything about either. In order for the Republic to be saved, the Jedi needed to destroy the Separatists and Palpatine at the same time. Either would be able to end the Republic. Of course, the Jedi didn’t really want to destroy Palpatine per se, as he’s incredibly valuable for the Republic war effort. They didn’t know just how many crimes he is responsible for and just how evil he is. In their eyes, even assuming ill intent, he’s at worst a greedy politician using the convenient crisis to grab more power. But let’s suppose they did find out who he really is. Yoda and Windu could probably take him down. They would still need to figure out how to win the war. The Separatist war machine can keep pumping out droids and droid ships and overwhelm the Republic. Without Palpatine holding them back, they would only be more undefeatable. The only way to defeat the Separatists is to kill their leaders. In what actually happened in the films, Palpatine felt the time was right, orchestrating the death of Dooku and then Grievous, leaving only the weaker Separatist leadership. Next, he executed Order 66, leaving only the useless Republic senate. Finally, he dealt the final blow to the Republic and Separatists at the same time and achieved domination. Destroying the Republic Destroying the Separatists The Jedi would have to do something similar. They would need to arrest or kill Palpatine, at the same time that they root out Separatist leadership. Unfortunately, it is IMPOSSIBLE to know where all the Separatist leaders are hanging out in such a large universe with literal millions of inhabited planets, and tens of millions of uninhabited planets (like Mustafar). Palpatine only managed because he was pulling the strings and knew everything. This is why I said they would need to be omniscient to save the Republic and themselves. They would need to know exactly how much of a threat Palpatine was, as well as know where all the Separatist leaders were. Sadly, Jedi are not omniscient. Quite the opposite, actually — they barely had any information. On the other hand, Palpatine did have all the information, which is why he won.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Would the programming for Order 66 have eventually been discovered if Palpatine had been removed from office halfway through the Clone Wars?
Answer: The programming for Order 66 is store in the inhibitor chips, nowhere else. The contingency orders were public knowledge. It was also common knowledge that you need to have protocols to verify that you are the Chancellor or the Chancellor’s office when issuing commands. If Palpatine issued an order to retreat from a planet, it would be the exact same protocols and authorization as issuing Order 66. The only unknown in all this, is the inhibitor chips that force the clones into killing Jedi. That’s the only special thing about Order 66. The effect and programming of the chip is only stored in each chip, and cannot be discovered. Even after knowing it was there, Ahsoka still had trouble finding it. So if Palpatine was removed from his office, all that would achieve is that now a new person in the Chancellor’s office who can activate the order. We are nowhere closer to uncovering the inhibitor chips. The only possible difference his removal from office makes, is if people close to Palpatine, like Mas Amedda, decided to rat him out. Many of them are opportunistic and might no longer be loyal to him if he falls. However, they would also know he’s a dangerous Sith lord, and would almost certainly not do so, if not merely for fear of their lives.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Was the rebellion against the Galactic Empire in Star Wars actually justified?
Answer: In what way would it not be justified? Political legitimacy The Empire is not legitimate. You might say, the Empire came about as a result of legal actions by the Republic’s governing body, the Senate. Sure, most of the senators were stupid or corrupt, but at least it was legal and totally democratic. And you would be utterly wrong. Let us refresh our memory on exactly how the Empire came about: The Republic was toppled in a coup, after a bloody civil war that the leader of that coup single-handedly brought about. Therefore, the Alliance to Restore the Republic (aka the Rebel Alliance) is legitimate and righteous in their cause to overthrow the traitorous Palpatine and restore the Republic. Moral high ground Obi-Wan is in the Rebel Alliance, so the Rebels have the moral high ground. I rest my case. In all seriousness, have you seen what the Empire does? In fact, we don’t even have to look at the genocides, the loss of rights and freedoms, and the low standards of living. Just look at how massive of a military they have. I think an effective way to visualize this is to describe what the real-world equivalent would look like. If the US became the Empire, they would have 10,000 aircraft carrier groups just to police the population (assuming every city is reachable by aircraft carriers). Every major city would have an army and marine garrison, fully equipped with tanks and heavy weaponry. What every other street corner would look like Strikes and protests that the army and marine garrison can’t deal with? Aircraft carriers would be sent, completely locking down the city. Troops would pour into the city. If that doesn’t work, sometimes the city would just be completely nuked, so extensively that even underground bunkers wouldn’t survive. Recently, the government has even finished construction on a station that would be able to easily decimate a city even more thoroughly than the aforementioned nukes, and has destroyed Chicago simply as a show of strength. If this was the country you lived in, would you want the Rebel Alliance to overthrow the government? Would you think it’s justified?

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Was Mon Mothma a terrorist?
Answer: A terrorist is someone who uses or advocates for terrorism. Terrorism, according to Dictionary.com, means “the unlawful use of violence or threats to intimidate or coerce a civilian population or government, with the goal of furthering political, social, or ideological objectives.” So let’s see if Mon Mothma fits the bill. Since she’s the leader of the Rebellion, and most of the major action undertaken by the Rebels have her support, if not her direct involvement. Therefore, we can simply see if the Rebels under her leadership commit acts of terrorism. “the unlawful use of violence or threats”, every military action the Rebels undertake, count as unlawful uses of violence. They also have threatened a fair share of Imperial officers and personnel. “to intimidate or coerce a civilian population or government,” I wouldn’t say the Rebels are trying to intimidate the Empire, rather they are more of trying to annoy the Empire. However, we can somewhat argue that their efforts are trying to coerce the government to capitulate, and to coerce the civilian population to support them and overthrow the government. “with the goal of furthering political, social, or ideological objectives.” I think this is self-explanatory. The Rebel Alliance is doing everything to overthrow the Empire and restore another political system, and hope the civilians in the Empire will rise up and oppose the Empire. As we can see, the Rebels, and by implication Mon Mothma herself, fits the definition of “terrorist”. We can even go a step further and liken the attack on the Death Star to the 9/11 attacks. I’m not arguing for who is right or wrong here, just comparing the two events without considering morality. 9/11 was a suicidal mission to destroy significant buildings, resulting in a massive number of civilian deaths and huge financial loss. It hurt the US deeply. The Death Star run was also a suicidal mission to destroy a significant building, resulting in a massive number of civilian deaths and huge financial loss. It hurt the Empire deeply. Therefore, even though most of us support the Rebels against the oppressive, authoritarian Imperial regime, I think we must admit: The Rebels, and their leaders like Mon Mothma, are terrorists. Often, the only difference between a freedom fighter and terrorist, is whether you agree with them or not. ;)

Question: Who would win in a war between Star Wars’s Galactic Empire and Halo’s Covenant?
Answer: The Covenant might be the galaxy’s big bully in the Halo galaxy, but will it match up against the big bully in the Star Wars galaxy? Let’s find out. Let’s start with the most important thing in warfare: Logistics and communication. Long story short, Covenant faster-than-light travel and communications are both through slipspace, while Star Wars travel is through hyperspace. Hyperspace is faster, safer, and more stable than Covenant slipspace. (Forerunner slipspace might be able to compete.) Star Wars communication is practically instantaneous, allowing people across the galaxy to have Skype calls with less lag than when I call my next-door neighbor. Covenant communication is limited by the speed of slipspace. Star Wars wins this easily. Now, for what you’re probably waiting for: their military prowess. Let’s start with their weaponry. I think a good place to start, is to look at their greatest feats of destruction. Orbital bombardment. Large ships in orbit above a planet bombard the planet surface with their giant plasma guns, each having destructive powers like nukes. Subsequently, this ends up destroying the planetary surface, boiling the oceans and melting the land. Both the Covenant and Galactic Empire could do this. Terrifying. In Halo, a good case to look at is Reach. The Covenant fleet at Reach was massive, consisting of over 300 ships (granted, most of them were small ships), and only glassed parts of the planet, mostly human population centers and military bases. It took this fleet around a month to glass “most” of the surface. Reach, after being glassed Furthermore, they only glassed the surface. You can still remove the stuff at the top, and terraform the planet to bring back an ecosystem. On the other hand, in the Star Wars universe, planetary bombardment could end up very deep, even sometimes destroying the entire planetary crust. One or two Star Destroyers would be able to completely melt a planet’s surface within a few hours. (If the planet doesn’t put up shields like Hoth.) It’s not even a close comparison. Using this as an estimate, a single Star Destroyer would at least have as much firepower as a small Covenant fleet. What about shields? Long story short, Star Wars shields are better, as they are made to withstand way better weaponry. I’m not going to expand on this, as the following section will make this pretty much irrelevant. The important thing is that a Star Destroyer could withstand bombardment from multiple Rebel capital ships and bomber squadrons at once. These capital ships are smaller and less powerful, but if you add up all the firepower, it’s at least on par with a Star Destroyer could do, and that is equivalent to a Covenant fleet’s capabilities. Hence, we can safely assume a Star Destroyer’s shield could hold against a Covenant fleet. Numbers and manpower The Covenant’s capital was known as High Charity, Its defense fleet had 500+ ships. This is probably the largest fleet in the Covenant. The fleet that invaded Reach had 300+ ships. Therefore, it’s reasonable to assume with all the various fleets the Covenant had, they likely had tens of thousands of ships, big and small. (Most are small ships.) High Charity and some of its defense fleet How many ships does the Empire have? Just counting Star Destroyers, the Empire had over 25,000. Previously, we estimated a single Star Destroyer is equivalent to a small Covenant fleet. So, 25,000 Covenant fleets. Even if we feel really generous and say a Covenant fleet is equivalent to five Star Destroyers, that’s still 5,000 fleets worth. The Covenant probably has 5,000 ships, but certainly not 5,000 fleets. After all, the Covenant only controlled “thousands” of star systems at the height of its power. Meanwhile, the Galactic Empire controlled twelve million, or 1,200 thousands, of star systems. The scale disparity is simply impossible to overcome. It’s not even remotely fair. The Empire waging war on the Covenant would be like an entire high school ganging up on a single kid.

Question: How did Padme call for a Vote of No confidence when she wasn't a senator?
Answer: “Call for” has two meanings. The first is what you’re thinking of. The other is where you state you want something, and urge other people to support it. It’s like how we can “call for tax reforms” or “call for a public inquiry” despite being mere civilians with no political power. Padme called for the vote in the latter sense. She told the Senate that she desires it, and she thinks the senators should support it. She’s not actually entering an official motion for the vote. If it came to that, any of the senators there could do it. Palpatine didn’t get Padme there to carry out the procedure for a Vote of No Confidence. He’s the senator of Naboo, he could do it. He needs Padme for the moral high ground, and to garner support for Naboo, and in extension, him. Name: Arthur Huan
Question: In Star Wars, why didn't Imperial Star Destroyers have escort ships the way that aircraft carriers here on Earth do?
Answer: There is one piece of technology in Star Wars that’s not here on Earth: Shields. I suppose you can say that our ships have armour, but their effectiveness doesn’t hold a candle to shields in Star Wars. One of the reasons battleships were phased out, is that even their powerful armour is not sufficient against planes. But if you look at the big capital ships in Star Wars, their shielding is more than enough. X-Wing fire, for example, could down an AT-AT, but would barely do anything to a Star Destroyer’s shields under normal circumstances. That’s why specialized bombers like the Y-Wing exist. (Or the very stupid B/SF-17.) Even then, you would usually need squadrons of these bombers, and you would need to find a way to get them past the TIE fighter screen and the point defences on the Star Destroyer. The Star Destroyers don’t need escort ships, as their shields allow them to take heavy fire. Oftentimes, an entire Rebel fleet’s worth of firepower wouldn’t be able to overwhelm a single Star Destroyer. In fact, not only are escort ships not necessary, they will actually be detrimental. Warfare in Star Wars is very different from our wars. The capital ships shouldn’t really be thought of as aircraft carriers, as aircraft carriers stay hundreds of miles away from the enemy ships and let their aircraft do the work. Meanwhile, in Star Wars, the ships are in each other’s faces blasting at each other. In this sense, capital ships are more like battleships. Of course, during WWII, battleships did have destroyer escorts, but they were mostly there for radar picketing or antisubmarine purposes. Neither is a thing in Star Wars. Besides, battleships could shoot over destroyers, since shells fly in an arc, and the battle is usually extremely spread out, so nobody really gets in each other’s way. In Star Wars, shots have to travel in a straight line. If Star Destroyers had escort ships, all they would do is get in the way and block shots, before their significantly weaker shields get overwhelmed and explode.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Why wasn't nanotechnology used as a weapon in Star Wars to control the galaxy?
Answer: Why wasn’t carbonite freezing utilized by Star Trek fleets? Why didn’t the Avengers use Death Stars to defeat Thanos? Why weren’t lightsabers used by Shrek to fight his foes? The answer to all the questions is: Different fictional universes have different things. Star Wars didn’t have weaponized nanotechnology. EDIT: Okay. Let’s go down the hard path. Star Wars does have nanotech. Star Wars even has nanotech that can be used destructively in war. However, I don’t think I’m wrong in saying there is no weaponized nanotech. Why? First, we need to establish a fundamental fact. Nanotech is a very broad term. Nanotech simply means the technology affects matter on a very small scale, among the realm of molecules and atoms. That’s all it is. It’s a very broad umbrella term. We already have nanotech. It’s used everywhere in industrial production, and we have nanotech all around us. Sunscreen has nanotech. Chips in our phones and computers have nanotech. Adhesives and paints utilize nanotech. So when you say something is nanotech, that’s as specific and useful as saying it is made from metal. Thus, the fact that Star Wars has nanotech says absolutely nothing about how useful it is for combat. Just because there is nanotech, doesn’t mean that can be utilized to make tools or war, because of how broad the term “nanotech” is. So far, the only kind of nanotech that could count as “weaponized” and destructive are the industrial nanodroids that could also set off explosions. They are quite dangerous, as they can be destructive, and don’t show up on scanners. But the way I see them, they’re just discrete explosives, not unlike what we already have. They could be useful in certain covert operations or assassins. They are certainly in no way near to a replacement for the real bigger grenades and explosives, the guns, the vehicles, and the ships.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Are most Star Wars fans biased when it comes to hypothetical fights against other franchises?
Answer: I would say most fans are biased when it comes to hypothetical fights against other franchises. Bias is inevitable. It’s the same bias that makes us think our sports team is performing better and deserves to win, even though the other side thinks so too. It’s the same bias that lets us overlook the flaws in our loved ones. The bias affects how people view hypothetical battles between all franchises, and isn’t special to only Star Wars fans. However, Star Wars fans might seem a bit more biased than other franchises’ fans, partially because how Star Wars isn’t always seen as sci-fi. The majority of Star Wars fans do not understand the science of Star Wars. A lot of it is made-up and fictional science, for sure, but as with any good fictional universe, there are still internal rules within that universe. There is still a system of fictional science and rules of physics in Star Wars. Unfortunately, most Star Wars fans don’t understand the rules. In a way, Star Wars is understood as a magical fantasy. The Force is just simply magic, and unconstrained magic at that. What happens is that most other fans will understand at least some of the limitations of their universes, while most Star Wars fans don’t seem to understand the limitations of the Star Wars universe. For example, take this answer I wrote in the past: I’ve seen so many people say Vader’s Force choke would just kill the Hulk, and even after I explained how the Force works and how strong the Hulk is, people still come to the comments and basically tell me that the Force is magic and Vader can suffocate the Hulk. His neck is stronger than anything Vader could hope to crush with his Force abilities. And Hulk literally doesn’t need to breathe. Even if Vader crushes his windpipe it doesn’t do anything. If you saw a Force choke as what it was — a way to telepathically exert a certain amount of force on a person’s neck — you wouldn’t suggest Vader’s Force choke is strong enough to choke the Hulk. He can’t exert the amount of force necessary. But if you saw the Force choke as a magical ability that allows you to simply choke your target to death, then sure, the Hulk is gonna get his ass whooped. Do note that I am not hating on or dismissing people who don’t understand the lore and see the Force as all-powerful magic. Star Wars lore isn’t easy to understand, it’s rarely central to the plot, and the material doesn’t fully explain everything to you. It’s normal to not understand the science of Star Wars. All I am saying is that this lack of understanding leads to an overestimation of Star Wars characters.

Question: What are some advantages/disadvantages of using a Chinese-style cleaver instead of an all-purpose chef knife for chopping vegetables, meat, etc.?
Answer: Just to get the record straight, I assume these are the two kinds of knives we’re talking about. For simplicity’s sake, I’ll call the latter the “knife” and the other one the “cleaver”, though both are chef knives with identical functions, just with different origins. (Also note there are different types of cleavers, but I won’t delve into that here.) Disadvantages of a cleaver They’re heavier and sometimes harder to maneuver compared to the lighter and smaller knives. On top of that, traditional Chinese chef knives would often use carbon steel, instead of stainless steel. That makes for a better cutting experience, but they also get rusty easier. Nowadays, most cleavers are made of stainless steel so this is a non-factor. Last but not least, cleavers don’t invoke the same kind of feeling of delicacy and elitism. They feel like what butchers use to carve out carcasses, not what chefs use to cook you a fine meal. That’s not completely accurate, but certainly understandable. Advantages of a cleaver Ever heard of how sharp premium Japanese chef knives are? Indeed they are. Well, premium Chinese cleavers come close. The more expensive Chinese chef knives’ sharpness is generally beneath Japanese ones but above German ones. Perhaps one of my favorite features, though, is that cleavers will generally have quite a bit of weight. While it’s a disadvantage for being heavier, it’s also sometimes an advantage, as that weight allows you to chop through tough foods. I’ve seen people use cleavers to chop straight through rib bones (though I suspect the blade was ruined afterward). Plus, it wouldn’t matter that much if your blade is dulled, as you’d still be able to cut using the blunt force that the heavier weight brings. Last but not least, cleavers are better hacking weapons. Though, I suppose this might not quite be such an advantage when it comes to people using them to massacre children in schools and kindergartens.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: In Star Wars II, Obi-Wan was puzzled by there being a gravity field, but no entry in the Jedi database, for planet Kamino - but since the Star Wars universe seems to have gravity on what should be weightless ships, isn't this cognitively dissonant?
Answer: The gravity on the ships are artificial gravity. The gravity is generated by technology. Before artificial gravity, if ships needed some sort of gravity, they’d spin and rotate. This is a similar concept as what ships did in movies like Interstellar and The Martian. The spinning generates forces that simulate gravity for the crew on board. It’s not some ridiculous space magic that just creates gravity out of nowhere. There are still laws of physics here. And regardless of how you’re generating this artificial gravity, the gravitational pull of the entire object itself on others is not bigger. The ship spinning merely makes it so that you feel weight while inside the spinning object, but the entire ship itself still has its original small mass, meaning a negligible gravitational field. Think of artificial gravity as like a way to metaphorically “strap” you to the ground of the ship. That’s all it does. It does not actually make the gravitational field equivalent to that of a planet.

Question: Is the butterfly keyboard the worst Apple product ever?
Answer: I think it’s not even a bad product. The butterfly keyboard is an ingenious design. I am dead serious. It’s full of innovation and creativity, and it feels really light to the touch. For anyone who doesn’t know about it (and that includes me about half an hour ago), butterfly keyboard isn’t referring to the shape of the keyboard or anything like that. It is referring to the shape of the switch underneath each key. Most laptop keyboards have scissor mechanisms, where two small plastic parts fit together in an x-shape to prop up the key. Apple invented the butterfly mechanism, where instead it looks almost like a very shallow V-shape. The reason the butterfly keyboard is better, in theory, is that the scissor mechanism tasks up a bit more space, and so the butterfly keyboard allows for a thinner keyboard, as well as requires less space for you to press down for a key to register. And I love it. I’ve never had the luxury of owning a Macbook, but typing on other people’s Macbooks that have butterfly keyboards just feels great. Before I talk about the great feel, let’s just talk about the drawback. The butterfly keyboard has one major drawback. It traps dust, debris, and food particles more easily. Then they could jam the keys. I have an easy solution for you: A keyboard cover solves the problem. In fact, I think even traditional scissor keys should have a keyboard cover. They still collect dust, and your fingers make the keys really dirty due to the natural excrement on your skin. Having a keyboard cover protects the keys and makes them convenient to clean. Now, on to the great feel of the butterfly keyboard. And just for reference, I am not a typist, but I do think I have a decent typing speed: And because this is NitroType, where I compete with other people in typing speed, I’m very particular about my keyboard. Here are four keyboards I’ve experienced, which helped me form my love for the butterfly keyboard. First, there is my HP laptop’s default keyboard, with the “trusty” scissor keyboard design. Except, as you can see, it’s not trusty at all: My “d” and “n” keys are missing. How? Well, the thin plastic frames in the scissor mechanism break too easily. They broke from just typing a few school essays, and within three months from purchase, my laptop didn’t have a functioning full set of keys on the keyboard. Next up, I have a Bluetooth keyboard, also using scissor mechanisms. Which sucks. This encompasses the greatest problems of the scissor mechanism, with a lot of space to press down and a lot of resistance. I sometimes miss letters because I didn’t press down hard enough, and my hands tire easily. Then there are basic classic keyboards in my university’s computer labs: They have way more space to press down. However, they are smother, and they’re desktop keyboards anyways. You’re supposed to pound down on them and feel the movement. It’s a different kind of keyboard from laptops. For this keyboard, I type more accurately and faster, but tire out quite quickly. Finally, there are MacBook butterfly keyboards. they're a joy to type on. They’re light and smooth, and I don’t tire out that easily. They check the boxes in everything you could want for a keyboard, apart from the desktop keyboard sounds. On my HP laptop’s broken keyboard, my speed is usually around 70 to 80 WPM, as I have to pause to press precisely on the switch when it comes to “d” and “n”, and that fear of missing the key slows down the whole thing process. On my Bluetooth keyboard, I hit around 90 to 100+ WPM. If I am confident and relaxed, I can hit over 110 WPM. On my school keyboard, I almost always hit over 100, but I can’t sustain it for long. I start out at 110 to 120, and quickly drop to 100 and then 90 within five minutes or so. On a MacBook keyboard, I hit 110+ easily, and for longer periods of time, as it doesn’t tire me out as much as the previous three keyboards. Now, I must admit, my perception of scissor keyboards is likely negatively skewed because I never tried any high-quality keyboards. All of these were much cheaper than Apple products. Though, I’ve also tried older MacBooks, with what I presume would be scissor keyboards, and felt they were less smooth. This confirms the butterfly keyboard’s theoretical superiority to me, and I’m satisfied. In conclusion, if you can use 1% of the money you spent on the laptop to buy a keyboard cover for it, you’ll solve most of the drawbacks, while enjoying a smoother and more satisfying typing experience. I think it’s a good product. Sadly, Apple has given up on it.

Question: Is it possible for black to win with the Italian variation of four knights chess?
Answer: Any opening that is somewhat sound will be winnable for both sides. As long as you don’t get mated right away, even if you sack your queen you could still win. I’ve had that kind of game before. That said, of course sacking your queen against an opponent of similar skill would be rather stupid. And certain openings make you end up with terrible positions. But rest assured that the Four Knights Game, Italian Variation is not unsound for Black. In fact, Black is slightly better here. This opening is considered a slight mistake on White’s part, as suddenly Black has more winning chances than White if played well. The top few lines all have Black having a better chance, but I’ll examine the vicious Nxe4, which is one of the reasons masters usually don’t play this opening as White. At surface level, it seems Black’s movie is a blunder, just giving White a knight for only a pawn. The e4 pawn seemed to be protected. And for most beginners and intermediate players, that's probably why they felt comfortable playing the bishop out to c4 in the first place. However, after Kxe4, Black simply has to play the obvious pawn move to d5: This forks the knight and bishop, thus immediately winning back the lost material. The best move for White after this actually isn’t to take with the bishop, as the Black queen is quite comfortable there, and white now has to play without a bishop into Black, who does. It was actually better to retreat the bishop, This certainly isn’t losing for either side, but Black is looking quite good, and it’s a better position than some other openings might have led to. So yes, it is very much possible for black to win with this opening. It’s actually quite good for Black, especially at higher levels.

Answer: All Chinese characters’ pronunciations have been lost to time. All of them. The characters we enunciate nowadays? Not how they were pronounced in more ancient times. For the most part, it’s probably still reasonably similar, but some characters could have been very different. This is why sometimes certain poems don’t sound as rhythmically pleasing or even rhyme. The sounds have been changed. Apart from pronunciations, many Chinese characters from ancient times are completely unknown. We simply do not know what the script is. After all, Chinese characters have transformed over all these thousands of years. The characters change and evolve. New things are invented and new characters and words pop up, while some others might disappear. Every now and then, a new system of text is implemented and the way all the characters are written, change. The characters did not stay the same. Some historical variations of the Chinese character 家, meaning “home” To figure out what a character traces to, or what they mean, we need to use clues from artifacts. For example, if the same literary work was passed down and then transcribed into a newer version of characters, and we know the newer characters, we can map the older ones. Or, if there are a large number of appearances of the same character, we might be able to use context clues to figure them out. But sometimes there just aren’t enough clues to piece together. Oracle text As you can imagine, the further back in history we go, the worse it gets. We know fewer bronze inscriptions than small seal script, and we know fewer oracle characters than bronze inscriptions, etc. In fact, barely half of all oracle script is known today. We have no idea what the remaining half is. Small seal script (The material also matters. Bronze inscriptions might be further back in history, but the bronze containers they were inscribed on would last way longer than the paper or cloth that some later texts are written on.) So yes, tons of Chinese characters have had their meanings lost to time, and all Chinese characters’ pronunciations have been lost to time.

Question: Which is the more "doable-in-real-life" Star Wars sci-fi weapon, the lightsaber or the blaster?
Answer: The blaster. It doesn’t violate the laws of physics. If the lightsaber was actually invented in real life, it would actually not be used as a weapon first and foremost. The technology would be used as our energy source. An almost infinite, perpetual source of energy? Sign me up. As you can tell, that is physically impossible. Something that small cannot give out so much energy all the time and does not have to be charged or replaced. They are not just perpetual machines, they are perpetual generators that generate massive amounts of energy considering their small size. Imagine an entire power plant powered in this fashion. We would never need to dig up a single liter of oil again. The blaster is, on the other hand, somewhat more reasonable. it fires bolts of plasma, and its ammunition has to be changed. In theory, it could work. You just need to find a way to turn the gas into plasma and then direct and propel the bolt. The only thing I find inaccurate is that the ammunition is stored in gaseous form, yet can last so long. As you can tell, gas is not very dense, so you’ll have very little gas for the same volume. People should be reloading all the time, not fire out hundreds of shots without having to reload. If the gas was instead stored in liquid or even solid state, then it’s way more believable that there could be that much stored in such a small volume.
