Question: What part of Qui-Gon Jinn's name is his given name?
Answer: Qui-Gon. Jinn is the surname. No matter what language or culture the name is from, in English the given name(s) always go before the family name(s). I come from China, and so in Chinese, my surname goes before my given name. However, the moment I use English to introduce myself or fill out a form, I need to switch it around. Though, there is another convention. The previous convention is used in mainland China, Japan, and Korea, and applies to every culture I know of so far. (Feel free to educate me on exceptions.) However, in Taiwan, they kept the translation tradition from all the way back in the Republic of China years. Sun Yat-Sen and Chiang Kai-Shek, for example, have their surnames in front. Sun Yat-Sen, or Zhongshan Sun This is still the case today with names like Tsai Ing-wen. So perhaps this rule isn’t absolute. Therefore, we have to go to the second clue, the fact that Qui-Gon has the dash between “Qui” and “Gon”. What this suggests is that “Qui” and “Gon” are two characters, which make up the whole given name. Jinn is the singular family name. “Qui-Gon” looks a lot like the same format as “Yat-Sen”. It’s also the same format as “Obi-Wan Kenobi”. We know Obi-Wan is his given name, and “Obi” and “Wan” are two separate characters from Japanese. It follows that Qui-Gon’s surname is “Jinn” and his given name is “Qui-Gon”. Though, it does seem a bit weird to me that the names don’t follow either convention. It should be either “Quigon Jinn” and “Obiwan Kenobi”, or “Jinn Qui-Gon” and “Kenobi Obi-Wan”.

Question: Is it rape if I take advantage of a drunk girl while I am drunk as well?
Answer: If you “take advantage of”, of course. But if you are drunk to the extent that you cannot give consent, which is what I think you’re driving at here, then you are also drunk to the extent that you cannot take advantage of someone. So the question should perhaps be rephrased to “Is it rape if I have sex with a drunk girl while I am also intoxicated?” There is rarely a clear-cut law addressing this. The law is almost always clear that if you know she cannot give consent, for instance, if she’s intoxicated, but yet you still engage in sex, then it’s rape. However, it’s usually vague on what to determine if both parties are drunk, at least for most of the places I know of. But let’s talk about this without reading into the words of laws. What should it be? If you have sex with a drunk girl, the drunk girl also had sex with the drunk you. So either the two people raped each other, or there was no rape. Either both people were rapists and victims at the same time, or there was no rape. To me, the latter feels more reasonable. Let’s also talk about consent. If you cannot think clearly enough to give consent and make the right decision, then surely you also cannot think clearly enough to understand the impossibility of the other person to give consent and make the right decision. So you could not have known that she cannot give consent. In this way, it would also mean it’s not rape. I’ll rest my case after one final point. If you tie up a random girl and rape her with her screaming no, that’s still obviously a crime. Being drunk doesn’t excuse criminal activities. However, statutory rape for having sex with an intoxicated person is not inherently a violent crime. It’s criminal only because you are conscious and taking advantage of their inability to make decisions. It’s exploitation. That’s why if you “take advantage” of her as stated in the question, it’s rape no matter what else you say. But if both people are intoxicated and unable to think straight, it’s no longer exploitation. This is akin to the fact that if an adult has sex with someone under the age of consent, it’s rape, but if both people are under the age of consent and reasonably close in age, often it’s not considered rape. The first is exploitation due to a difference in maturity and power dynamic. The second is not. I rest my case.

Question: Does Obi-Wan Kenobi have any real character flaws?
Answer: The only character without flaws are badly written ones, and you can quote me on that. And as a well-written important character, Obi-Wan also has this thing called “character arcs”, so many of his flaws change and develop over time. (Static characters certainly can work, but usually only for less important characters. Windu being static was perfectly fine, for example.) Just a few examples of Obi-Wan’s flaws: Padawan Obi-Wan was headstrong He was brash, headstrong, and outspoken. Perhaps it’s magnified in contrast to the calm and collected demeanor of Qui-Gonn, but I found padawan Obi-Wan almost similar to Anakin’s attitude as an apprentice. Of course, we saw him grow out of this very quickly and become one of the calmest Jedi we get to see. Obi-Wan was reluctant to demonstrate trust in Anakin Of course, it’s rather hard to trust someone like Anakin, so I can’t exactly fault Obi-Wan. However, openly stating doubt in Anakin’s abilities is going a bit too far. He could have encouraged Anakin for improvements, with a decent dose of reminders for humility. Instead, there were only the reminders for humility, and Anakin responded by being a rebellious teen that didn’t take these reminders. Later, Obi-Wan went in the opposite direction and had too much faith in Anakin instead. Again, I cannot fault him for this either, after going through so much with Anakin and seeing the growth over all the years. But he grew. He learned to trust and let go, and believed in Luke. Perhaps too much trust, though it worked out in the end. Obi-Wan was always set in his ways and unable to change easily Once Obi-Wan makes up his mind about something, he doesn’t get over it or change his mind easily. He’s exceedingly stubborn in his ways of thinking. He was convinced Anakin is the Chosen One and must be trained. He was convinced that he was at fault for Anakins’ fall and is depressed and broken. He was convinced that Luke should be trained instead of Leia, for seemingly little reason. This is sometimes a a good thing, but often not. It’s a flaw that has caused him much strife. These aren’t all, but it suffices to show that Obi-Wan certainly does have flaws. He has to, or he’s not a convincing character. He’s also a dynamic character with a lot of depth, and his flaws and virtues changed and morphed throughout the years.

Question: Are there any real cities with multiple inhabited levels, or even levels in general, similar to Coruscant in Star Wars?
Answer: Yes, though not quite the same. Three years ago, I went UWC Selection Day (Spoiler Alert, I got admitted). All the applicants were divided into groups to go through the day. One of the most outspoken and dominant people in our group was a girl who I will denote as V in this answer. Later, I added V on social media and we chatted a bit. I don’t know how the conversation went, but somehow it came around to me suggesting (jokingly) that maybe I should visit her at her hometown. She said “Oh no, that would be a terrible idea.” “Why?” “Because you’ll get lost.” “I have Baidu Maps.” “Baidu Maps won’t help you much here.” And then she sent me a meme. Two people were meeting up. One person arrived, and after waiting and waiting, decided to call the other. “Where are you? I arrived and waited for fifteen minutes.” “What? I arrived too, where are you?” “I’m on the first floor!” “Huh? I'm on the first floor too!” The GPS showed they were in the same place, but apparently, they were on different “first floors”. V told me that there in her city, not only did you often have to climb a lot, you often didn’t even know where you’re supposed to go with all the layers. Even some locals aren’t perfectly capable of navigating the layers and complicated net of roads, bridges, and above-ground and below-ground floors. Her hometown is the city of Chongqing, one of the four Chinese municipalities that are at the same level as provinces. (The other three are Beijing, Shanghai, and Tianjin. All are absolutely massive and affluent.) Not this though. This part is like most other cities and not layered. I mean parts of Chongqing like this: Parts of Chongqing that are built on mountains, with the roads and buildings often overlapping each other. The roads and layers are so complicated that map apps have practically given up. This is the closest example of a Coruscant-like city in real life that came to my mind.

Question: Is it always the case that the best chess player in the world is a man?
Answer: There is nothing stopping a woman from becoming the best chess player in the world. Chess is not segregated by gender. So now the question is, did it happen? The best female chess player in history has to be Judit Polgár, undisputedly. (The Polgár sisters have an insane backstory, by the way. I didn’t even know about it until reading about it in Atomic Habits.) She is the only woman to have ever even had a shot at the World Champions, having attended the World Chess Championship in 2005. She placed 8th. This was the year she hit her peak rating of 2735. This is hugely impressive for a woman in chess. For reference, the current best female player, Hou Yifan, …is only rated 2650. That places her at 98th place on the FIDE rankings, and not even a super GM. Oh, did I also mention Hou Yifan happens to hold the second highest peak rating just behind Judit Polgár? She hit 2686 in 2015. Even then, she was still not at super GM status. So yes, the best chess player in the world has always been a man. Judit Polgár was the only person who came even remotely close to changing that, but even she still had a ways to go. All the other female players never even hit super GM status, let alone had a shot at being considered the best chess player.

Question: Who is Darth Maul? Is he a Sith Lord? If so, why did Palpatine say that there were only two Sith Lords in existence at the time of his arrival on Naboo?

EDIT: OK, issue of Plagueis. There is a distinction between canon and Legends to be made here. In Legends, the Rule of Two is not strictly upheld. It’s routine for Sith Apprentices to go behind their master’s backs and train their own apprentices. Sometimes they don’t call the secret apprentice Sith, like with Starkiller. Sometimes they do, like with Darth Maul. As such, often there are violations of the Rule of Two. Sidious training Darth Maul, while he himself was Sith Apprentice, is one such violation. In canon, the Rule of Two has so far never been confirmed to be broken. Plagueis’s death in Legends is not canon. We do not know when Sidious killed his master. Thus, we don’t know if the Rule of Two was ever broken. It’s highly likely that Plagueis died before Sidious took on Maul. Or Sidious only started calling Maul a Sith after he killed his master. Or perhaps Sidious simply breached the Rule of Two. It’s not unthinkable.

Question: Can the average man play Chess blindfolded?
Answer: No. (Source) It might seem easy for the top dogs, but blindfold chess is actually pretty hard, and a significant handicap. I’d be surprised if good club players could play blindfold chess well without having practiced it deliberately. I am in the top 10% of Rapid players on Lichess, and I am not even able to play three moves blindfolded. I might be lacking in this respect compared to my peers, but I am certain I am not lacking so much that I’d be worse than the average man at blindfold chess. It is very difficult and requires good memory, visualization skills, and understanding of positions and patterns in chess. EDIT: Perhaps I should mention something that I was reminded of when playing with Julia Ziebart last night. I have aphantasia, “mind blind”. When I close my eyes, it’s complete nothingness and I cannot imagine anything. I thought this was the norm until I stumbled upon an article about aphantasia. Apparently, the complete absence of all the senses (sight, taste, hearing, smell, touch) is not normal. I am not sure how useful it is to see a vague image of the board and pieces in your mind’s eye, but if it is, my inability to see anything might be a factor here. Regardless, it’s still very hard to do blindfold chess, especially for the average player, who doesn’t have as strong pattern recognition of various positions as masters. Thus I still stand by my original answer.

Growing up, being black, and wanting to be an artist — which is a very challenging and brave thing to do, it’s not easy — we’re always faced, as black artists, with this idea of being a sellout. Question: How many multiples of 3 lie between 150 and 450?
Answer: Here is a neat mental trick that will make questions like this trivial. Imagine the sequence of numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7… 42. Do you know how many numbers there are? That’s right, 42. Now imagine the sequence of numbers 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21… 126. Do you know how many numbers there are? It seems more complicated than the previous question, but is it? If you divide each number by three, the sequence becomes 1, 2, 3, 4… 42, just like before. And because you only divided every number, the number of numbers in the sequence didn’t change. Thus you know that there were 42 multiples of 3 between 3 and 126, inclusive. Now what happens when you have 150 and 450? You can do the same thing and divide by 3. So now you’d be asking how many multiples of one there are between 50 and 150. If you know this problem, you can simply do 150–50+1=101 numbers. If you don’t, or want a way to verify, do the same thing we did before, but this time with subtraction. Subtract 49 from all the numbers, and you end up with a sequence of numbers from 1 to 101. Thus there are 101 numbers. This is a very powerful tool to quickly figure out how many multiples of a certain number there are between two numbers.

Question: Where do you prefer to play online chess more: lichess.org or chess.com?
Answer: My answer history would be a guide to it. My earlier answers always featured positions screenshotted from the Chess.com analysis board, but recently all of them came from the Lichess analysis board. And here’s why I made the switch. #1 - Lichess is free Now, I understand that free software is not always better, and open source is slightly overhyped. However, they are still wonderful, and good programs like LibreOffice, VLC, and Mozilla Thunderbird are mainstays in my device. Lichess is one such good program. It’s clean, smooth, and rich in features. I also don’t find any privacy concerns, ads, or other common issues. Chess.com offers free live chess matches, and that’s it. I cannot do puzzles or access lessons. I also didn’t like how they went from being free to having more and more stuff locked behind paywalls over time. It’s become less serviceable over time Lichess is free, and it’s great. There is very little Chess.com does intrinsically better. #2 - Better playing experience On Chess.com — and I am not exaggerating when saying this — one in three opponents when faced with a losing position, will refuse to resign and run down their clock. Stalling is not allowed and is reportable. However, this still keeps happening. Lichess somehow doesn’t have this phenomenon. Perhaps it is this warning that helps. Furthermore, I love this time control: 10-minute games are too rushed, and 30-minute games are too long. 15 minutes is perfect for me. I do know that Chess.com also supports 15-minute games, but it’s not a default option and few players seem to play it. #3 - Game modes You might be surprised to hear that Lichess has better support for some variants. Especially when I need to play antichess with my girlfriend so that she can finally enjoy the thrill of taking all of my annoying pieces. Chess.com does also have antichess, but I cannot invite people to play me at will. There are restrictions. A few good words for Chess.com Of course, Chess.com isn’t inferior to Lichess in every way. Firstly, I like Lichess interface better, but others could see it differently and prefer Chess.com. The latter does have more customization. It’s subjective. Other than that, I think Chess.com also has much better PR. It has a better name, good news feed, a massive presence on Twitch, and is just more influential. They partner with more tournaments and have more creators that partner with them. Of course, a lot of this comes from having a lot of money, which is not something Lichess has access to. In terms of gameplay, I prefer the Chess.com premoves. You can’t premove that well on Lichess. Though, I don’t play blitz, so the premoves don’t matter to me anyway.

Question: How is it that the best human chess players are unable to even draw against the top AI players now? Shouldn't drawing the game be easier than winning?

Question: What real world military unit would Imperial Stormtroopers be most comparable to?

Question: Is it possible to win in chess without capturing the king?

Question: Can all the computers in the world solve the game of chess when brought together?
Answer: Let’s look at how hard the task is. Just for the 1st move, each player has 20 possible moves, totaling 400 possible board setups. For the next moves, there are even more options, but let’s assume 20 for every move. That would be 400*400=160,000. The real number is much larger, over 190,000, but I don’t care that I am lowballing it. After just the 3rd move, by this calculation, there would be 64 million possible setups. The real number is almost twice that. But again, I don’t care that I am lowballing the number so much. Why? Because even with this method that drastically underestimates, if we go to just 10 moves, we have 104 septillion possibilities. 104,857,600,000,000,000,000,000,000. For reference, we only have 7.5 septillion grains of sand on Earth in total. Let’s go to 20 moves, shall we? By 20 moves, there’d be an estimated 10 to the power of 52 possibilities by this method, Over 10 sexdecillion possibilities. The number is so large that spellcheck doesn’t even think this is a proper word. It would be ten quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion quadrillion possibilities — by only move 20. Now imagine what happens when you go to 40 moves or even longer. I could crash Quora’s server by the number of “quadrillion”s I’d be trying to type in. This is the power of exponential growth. In fact, while we are on the topic of chess, this is the story I heard when my dad introduced me to the concept of exponential growth. A king challenged a mathematician to a game of chess, and if the mathematician could win, the mathematician could choose his reward. To the king’s surprise, the mathematician didn’t ask for half the kingdom or the princess’s hand like every other fairytale hero. He simply asked for grains of rice, the amount of which would be determined by a simple algorithm. On the first square on the chess board, place 1 grain of rice. Each subsequent square would be doubled, so 2 for the next, 4 for the next, and so on. The total amount would be his reward. The king thought a few grains of rice would be like nothing to him. But when he lost and the mathematician asked for the reward, he realized that by the 64th square, the number was so astronomical that there isn’t enough rice on the entire Earth. So the king had to kill the mathematician. So I don’t think we should be the king and underestimate the power of exponential growth, especially when by the 3rd move there are already 120 million possible board setups for a chess game. There is no possibility to solve chess. NOTE: You might be wondering, what if we don’t brute force it? What if we could look at only some positions? After all, most of these positions would be ridiculous. Good question. I like the critical thinking. Though, we have these algorithms already, in engines like Stockfish. Besides, even if chess is solvable, we don’t need to. Stockfish, given only 1 millisecond to think on each move, already plays almost perfect chess. In 0.1 milliseconds, the engine can see complicated variations like the one at 2:25 in the following video by Levy. “Almost perfect” should be good enough for us. We don’t need to have chess solved.

The pawn diamond is an upgrade on this structure: which is generally considered a good structure, though usually not as good as a pawn chain without more information on the opponent’s structure. A pawn diamond would seemingly be much better, as your opponent would have to somehow infiltrate your ranks and bring a piece behind to attack the last pawn, which is the diamond’s biggest weakness. It would be considerably hard to do so compared to attacks from the front. Another option for the opponent is to use pawns to chip away at the diamond: But then, you’d just end up with something like the following: Neither of which are bad in themselves. As for the diamond’s offensive potential, it’s pretty good. You have only one backwards pawn, and that pawn is still able to effectively support the three forward pawns. I would say that in certain endgame situations, it would even be better than four pawns spread out in a chain. Your king might not be able to cover for all four pawns. However, a pawn diamond is more compact and the king just has to cover one to two pawns at a time while you shuffle forward. At least that’s what I think. It’d be interesting to hear more from other people.

Question: It is said in Star Wars the Clone Wars season 2 episode 12 the Darksaber was stolen from the Jedi Temple since the fall of the ancient Republic, meaning it was first created by the Jedi, why didn't the Jedi or Sith make more Darksabers?
Answer: Imagine if the Rosetta Stone was stolen. Should we get people to make a new one? I’m sure there is enough information about the Rosetta Stone that we can make a very similar replica. It could almost be identical. Then, we could put it back in the British Museum for people to come to look at it. Heck, we could make many more and put the stones in museums all around the world! But, does that accomplish anything? The Rosetta Stone isn’t necessary for our society to function, and it’s not better than other slates, papers, or electronic documents for issuing things to the public. The Rosetta Stone is only valuable because of its historic value. And evidently, any replica wouldn’t have the same historic value, so it would be pointless to make them. In the same way, the Darksaber is only valuable due to its historic value. It was crafted by Tarre Vizsla, the first Mandalorian to be a Jedi. Later, it became a symbol of power and was wielded by many Mandalorian rulers. That is it. The Darksaber isn’t a special lightsaber otherwise. The Jedi have no need to make a new one, just as we don’t need to make a new Rosetta Stone. Moreover, it would be pointless. The new Darksaber wouldn’t be special, as it doesn’t have the history. (Also, I’m not sure if this is canon or Legends, but I read that Tarre Vizsla is the only one who was able to turn the kyber crystal black. Question: In the star wars prequels, Palpatine has the clones given a built in set of standing orders. Who knows what the full list is? Also who is authorized to issue those orders?

And yes, Order 69 is unfortunately also non-canon). Authorization of these orders can come from two sources: Now, that sounds really problematic, to think a single person or a single committee in the senate could issue drastic orders like Order 66 to the Republic’s massive army. That is, until you remember that in our world, nuclear weapons also only require one person to authorize. But that doesn’t mean that one person single-handedly controls the nuclear weapons. Besides, even if the standing orders didn’t exist, Palpatine could just call up the clone commanders and give them the orders. He has that authority. There’s no reason the standing orders are anything more than a compilation of important orders and action plans that the clones learn in advance. The idea is that when something happens, they’d know what to do. It’s not dissimilar to our standing orders or contingency plans. Unfortunately, the inhibitor chips changed this whole dynamic.

Question: Do you think Darth Sidious secretly used his powers to help the ship land “safely” back on Coruscant? Would he leave his survival to chance like that?

On a micro level though, he rarely has complete control, especially as most of the time he can’t use his Force powers. If he did use his Force powers on the half of the Invisible Hand, for example, Anakin and Obi-Wan would likely have felt it. And then, his cover is blown, and his chances are much lower than trying to survive through the ship crash. But of course, he didn’t need to do anything to begin with. Palpatine might not have intervened, but he did NOT leave it to chance. Notice that I said he resigned himself to his destiny of success? When we resign ourselves to fate or to our destiny, we are helpless. For us, that would be “leaving it to chance”. But not for Palpatine. He often knows his destiny, courtesy of the foresight that the Force granted him. Of course, he isn’t omniscient about the future, but he does see most, if not all, of the important things. His unfortunate demise on the Invisible Hand would have been one of these things. So, Palpatine simply resigned himself to the destiny he already foresaw. He knew he would survive, and he knew he would succeed at vanquishing the Jedi. It was all certain, and even though he didn’t intervene, it was assured. Ironically, in the end, his confidence was misplaced when it came to Luke and Vader/Anakin. And perhaps it was this overconfidence and hubris which led to his ultimate defeat. His preminitions served him well all these years, and saved him from close calls and assassination attempts. Yet, it did not aid him when it came to the two most important Force users in the galaxy.

Question: Who gave King Arthur his sword Excalibur and why did he need it in first place?
Answer: There are two famous mythical swords associated with King Arthur. The sword in the stone, and Excalibur. In some versions, the two are separate. In some versions, they are the same sword. In the versions where Excalibur and the sword in the stone are the same, it would be Merlin who indirectly gave the sword to Arthur. Merlin was the one who set up the challenge, with the sword set in the stone. It was said that the one who could pull it out would be king. Arthur was the only one who was able to achieve this. In the version I know, he did it by accident as an errand (he was a squire at the time). Later, he repeated it publically and thus claimed his throne. This sword was later revealed to be called Excalibur. In another version, Excalibur and the sword in the stone are different swords. As far as I am aware, this is also the most common version nowadays. The story of the sword in the stone as told above is the same, but the sword wasn’t named Excalibur. Instead, Arthur got Excalibur from the Lady of the Lake. King Arthur was fighting a battle with the old sword from the stone, whereupon Merlin took him to a lake. There, King Arthur saw a hand holding a sword above the water. It was Excalibur, and the hand belonged to the Lady of the Lake. King Arthur retrieved the sword, and it became his weapon for the rest of his life. In some telling of the story, the sword is magical and made it so that King Arthur never lost a single battle when wielding it. (Which really begs the question of why other knights would be held in greater regard for their combat abilities when Arthur himself was nigh invincible.) So in this version, it was the Lady of the Lake who gave him the sword, with Merlin as a guide.

However, he’s won the mental battle, and he’s making it very clear. He’s also showing Vader the possibilities, as well as forcing Vader’s hand by putting himself in harm’s way. Luckily, in the end, the gamble paid off. In short, once Luke got hit by the lightning it was a bit too late to do anything. Question: Why is the rook in chess allowed to be called a tower but not a castle?
Answer: I’ve never heard anyone call it a “tower”, while many called it a “castle”. Officially, the rook is not allowed to be called anything other than “rook”, unless in a language other than English. For example, in Chinese, the rook is called 车/車, meaning “chariot”, taking after its equivalent in Xiangqi. I imagine that in some other language, the rook could indeed be called something that means “tower”, because the rook is indeed just a tower in a castle. Otherwise, in English, “rook” is the official and most common way to go. And if you don’t call it that, both “castle” and “tower” should both be okay for unofficial communication so long as the other person understands what you mean.

Question: What is the most annoying chess move?
Answer: For me, the most annoying chess move is when your opponent gives you a free piece out of nowhere. Of course, I love it when my opponent hangs a piece, but not when they give me a free piece out of nowhere. “If it’s too good to be true, it probably is.” It’s one thing if they fall for a trap or just overlook a threat. But it’s another when they hang a piece very obviously, because then, 9 times of 10 it’s a trap. The most obvious trap would be something like this: You can’t just take the “free” knight, because then Black can play Re1# mate. But some traps are less obvious, and you have to wrack your brain to find it. Take the following position, for example: I am playing Black, and just played cxd4. What will you play as White? Probably Qxd4, right? Then I will follow up with Bc5, kicking the queen away. Then I will have a better position. My pieces will be better developed, and I have a good control over the center. But these are just my thoughts. Let’s get back to the position first, and see what the opponent will do. I wait. It’s been 30 seconds already. Not much to do except wait. The opponent’s clock keeps ticking down. 1 minute gone. 1 minute and 30 seconds. … As I press Ctrl+T and open Quora, I hear the familiar sound of a move. I click back, and see this: I briefly looked at this line before, and it seemed so terrible for White that I didn’t think it was worth considering. I encourage you to pause and have a short think if you haven’t found the move yet. Anyway, I was shocked. “Huh? Can’t I just Rxc1+ and win a free bishop? And then a free rook or a queen-rook trade?” I thought. It’s too obvious, so I’ve evidently missed something. If it’s too good to be true, it probably is. Surely, my opponent has set up an elaborate trap for me, but I can’t see any. I am excited. I square up for the challenge, and settle into a long think, looking for the trap. I will find the opponent’s hidden devious intentions and be one step ahead. Soon, the excitement turns into agony and frustration. I can’t see it. I just can’t. It’s more annoying than realizing you are in a mate in 3, because then you can see what the opponent will do and resign to them and to your fate. You can then go away and marvel at what they did and learn from it. In contrast, these moments when your opponent evidently is planning something, but you can’t see what they want to do, now these moments are very annoying. It’s even more annoying when you realize the long think was over nothing. There was no trap. There was no hidden devious plan or anything you can learn from — your agony was over nothing. They simply hung their pieces.

Question: Is the Darksaber heavier than a lightsaber?
Answer: No. Though, it is quite “heavy”, much heavier than most would expect. The Darksaber is just like any other lightsaber in its structure. There’s little difference in weight. Most crucially, the blade of a lightsaber is plasma, which is a form of gas. It’s basically an exceedingly hot blade of air. There is almost no weight in a lightsaber’s blade, which is where it matters the most for a sword’s weight. So, no, the Darksaber is not heavier than any other lightsaber. The Darksaber, like all other lightsabers, weighs very little, with an almost weightless blade. Why then, did Din struggle? Is the Darksaber actually heavy? To this, I say yes. The Darksaber, like all other lightsabers, is actually quite “heavy”. They weigh almost nothing but are also quite heavy. This is because “heavy” doesn’t always mean “weighs a lot”. For instance, take the sentence “My eyelids grew heavy and I soon dozed off.” My eyelids aren’t actually gaining more weight. They don’t weigh more, but they are perceived as “heavy” because it’s hard for me to keep them open. In the same way, even though lightsaber blades are weightless, they are heavy because they are hard to control. The reason Din struggled to wield the Darksaber is the same as why Sabine struggled. When Sabine turned on the Darksaber, she remarked “It’s heavier than I expected. To which, Kanan replied, Energy constantly flows through the crystal. You are not fighting with a simple blade as much as you are directing a current of power. Your thoughts, your actions, they become energy. They flow through the crystal as well and become a part of the blade. While some interpret this as evidence that the Darksaber weighs more than a normal lightsaber, I disagree. First, I think we would all agree that the Darksaber doesn’t weigh more, as energy doesn’t have weight. Second, this is a characteristic that all lightsabers have. Kanan is not a Mandalorian historian explaining special features of the Darksaber. He is a Jedi explaining the properties of a lightsaber to someone who is unfamiliar. This thing about energy? It applies to all lightsabers. After saying the above quote, Kanan ignited his own lightsaber to keep explaining. This suggests what he is saying applies to all lightsabers, and is the reason on my first watch, I interpreted it as such. Furthermore, I present to you, Windu and Vaapad. Vaapad is a mindset, where the user is able to channel their inner darkness, and where a true master can even use their opponent's dark side and channel it back at them. Yet, Vaapad is a lightsaber form, which sounds a bit weird. It makes sense if a lightsaber form is about defense, or about acrobatics combined with offensive strikes, or if it’s about counterstriking. However, it doesn’t make sense to say a lightsaber form is about “using the dark energy in you” or “channeling your opponent’s energy back at them”. And it certainly doesn’t make sense that a lightsaber can direct Force lightning back at the user in a loop when wielded by a Vaapad user. Unless… Energy does actually affect the lightsaber and constantly flows through the Kyber crystal. It makes sense if the user’s thoughts and actions become energy and flow through the lightsaber too. Sound familiar? This is exactly what Kanan explained. He meant it for all lightsabers, not just the Darksaber. The only things that make the Darksaber special are its aesthetics and its history. It doesn’t actually have any other special properties. It’s not hotter, more magnetic, or heavier. The Darksaber is just as light or heavy as other lightsabers, and all lightsabers are heavy if you are unfamiliar with the energy within them and how to direct the energy.

Question: What if dinosaurs were teleported to a Star Wars planet like Tatooine or Hoth?
Answer: The dinosaurs would die. Have you ever heard about altitude sickness? When you cannot get enough oxygen from the air, you become very sick, and could even die if serious. Have you also heard about oxygen toxicity? When you get too much extra oxygen from the air, you become very sick, and could even die if seirous. Have you also heard about starvation? When you don’t get enough food for too long, you die. Have you also heard about climate’s importance for animals? There is a reason lions don’t live in the Arctic. Have you also heard about animals needing to be in an ecosystem to survive? If you have heard of all the above, you’ll know just a few of the reasons why dinosaurs would die very quickly if they are teleported to a Star Wars planet like Tatooine or Hoth. No Star Wars planet would have the right concentration of oxygen in the air, the right kinds of food, the right climate, and the ecosystem to support any dinosaurs. Not even the smallest and most resilient ones.

Question: Would Vader cover up his face with a mask even if he didn't have the injuries of Mustafar, just to hide his former identity as Anakin Skywalker?

So when Palpatine comes out to say the Jedi were traitors and tried to take over, and then Anakin backs him up, it’s perfect. Anakin being well-liked means the Empire will also be more liked and seem more legitimate. The duel on Mustafar leading to Vader having to don a mask was a setback, because now Palpatine lost a great piece of propaganda material. However, he did manage to be flexible and change his plans. With the original plan spoiled, he quickly changed to instead making Vader as imposing and terrifying as possible. It was a compromise and Palpatine making the best out of an unfortunate situation, not the original plan. If Vader had not been so heavily scarred on Mustafar, he would no doubt have gone around with his face shown to everyone, as a great piece of propaganda for the Empire.

Question: In the Obi-Wan series, why didn't Vader stop Obi-wan’s attacks with the force like he did with the 3rd sister?
Answer: An easy way to approach this is to think of the strengths as numbers, like in a video game. Each person has a number for their innate natural strength. Let’s just arbitrarily say Vader has 5, Reva has 3, and Obi-Wan has 4. Because they are Force users, they can also use the Force to either push something with telekinesis or enhance their strength. Let’s say Vader has 20, Reva has 12, and Obi-Wan has 18. When Reva tries to push on her lightsaber, she is using both her innate strength and the Force. So the amount of strength she puts behind that lightsaber is 3+12 = 15. Vader uses the Force alone, 20. 20 is much higher than 15 so his Force push is more than enough to match her. But what about Obi-Wan? When Obi-Wan uses both his strength and the Force, it would be 4+18 = 22. Now Vader’s Force push alone, 20, isn’t enough. Obi-Wan and Vader are similar in strength with the Force. Their difference in Force is small enough that Obi-Wan’s physical strength bridges the gap. Even if Obi-Wan using his strength and the Force together isn’t enough to overpower Vader’s Force push, it will definitely make Vader struggle. Then it wouldn’t be efficient to use the Force alone on Vader’s part. It would cost him much less to whip out his lightsaber and parry, so he can use his own strength too. It’s like if I try to race with Usain Bolt, it wouldn’t matter if he has to wear some weights around his waist. The handicap doesn’t matter much because I’m too puny and weak. But if Usian Bolt is racing Justin Gatlin, then he would certainly not want the weights. Reva is like me. She is not anywhere strong enough to cause Vader any problems, even if he has a handicap and uses a less efficient way to stop her.

Question: What happens when you attempt to pierce a mirror with a lightsaber?
Answer: The mirror gets burned and melted. I can guess where this is coming from, but unfortunately, a lightsaber is not a sword of “light” or a laser sword. So the mirror wouldn’t reflect it. A lightsaber is made of plasma, which is a type of matter. The plasma would simply burn and melt the mirror. As a bonus, even if a lightsaber was made of lasers, the mirror still gets destroyed. A mirror doesn’t actually reflect all the light. It still absorbs some of the light, so the laser would still affect it. A high-powered laser that can cut through steel like a knife through butter will have enough energy to destroy the mirror too.

Question: If it is often claimed that Darth Vader was indeed much more powerful in the Dark Side of the Force than Anakin Skywalker, himself, had been, then does that mean Darth Vader's midichlorian count was actually somewhat higher than Anakin's? If so, how?
Answer: Of course Vader would be more powerful in the dark side of the Force than Anakin. Anakin used the light side of the Force, not the dark. Regarding the Force in general, of course it’s still the case that Vader would be stronger than Anakin. Imagine you have an empty glass. You fill it with water. If you have the same glass, you can still have varying amounts of water. If you filled it halfway, you can keep pouring in more water for there to be more water. You wouldn’t have to get a larger glass to get more water. This is the same for Vader and Anakin. The Force potential is like the empty glass’s potential to be filled with water. You train to fill it up. Vader is stronger than Anakin, because he kept on filling the glass. So he is more connected to the Force and stronger with it. So no, Vader doesn’t have a higher Force potential than Anakin. He simply trained longer and grew up more, to realize more of his potential.

Question: How much worse would Return of the Jedi have been if Lucas kept the original ending (Luke taking his father's mask on)?
Answer: I would not think it would be worse. It would be grittier and more depressing, but more interesting. It would also leave the story in suspense and set up for a future story. Luke, so far, had been following a pretty standard hero’s journey. He persevered and showed that staying true to good works. He even managed to find the good in his father that nobody else saw, and pulled off a redemption. Anakin killed Palpatine, the Death Star blew up, and everything was good. Everyone lived happily ever after. Except, nobody lived happily ever after, as Sith Luke came back and slaughtered the Rebels. Leia wasn’t there, so she survived, and after killing his former friends, Luke has now become as irredeemable as Vader. (Which is still a little redeemable, evidently). Perhaps he can be the one to kill Han. It would make an emotional moment and raise the stakes, as well as a callback to the moment Anakin killed the younglings. One moment that shows there is no going back and the dark side is making the person go into a craze. It’s much grittier, grimmer, and interesting, at least for me. There is a lot to explore further down the line. Some potential plotlines could be: Leia would be a great strong female lead, if that was the point of Rey. Luke would be a better villain than Kylo Ren. We get to see Luke and Leia, at their primes with realized Force potential. We get to see a the New Republic and New Jedi Order, and how they learn from past mistakes. And so much more. Not only would Return of the Jedi be slightly better, but the Sequels would also probably be better too.

Question: Which would win, Star Wars weapon and armor tech vs Halo weapons and armor tech?
Answer: I’d like to separate “weapon” and “armor” techs, and look at them individually. Do be warned though, as I am a bigger Star Wars fan, I am somewhat biased towards Star Wars. Armor I don’t think I can overstate how awesome Halo armor is. Spartans with their armor can usually take multiple shots from projectiles and plasma alike. Plus, the armor compliments the Spartans’ superhuman speed and strength, and houses smart AI, so the armor is a deadly suite of great defense and offense. Star Wars armor also protects against projectiles, which is partially why slugthrowers are supposedly ineffective now. However, as rocks slung from slingshots could kill or at least stun troopers with the armor, I don’t think it’s that good. And, the blasters always penetrate armor easily. Bolts of plasma are evidently too much for Star Wars armor, rendering them useless. However, Spartan armor (even without shields) can take multiple plasma bolts with no issue, as stated above. Though, there is an exception. Beskar armor is even better than the Spartan armor. Beskar can withstand lightsabers and blaster bolts for a very long time. Spartan armor cannot hope to compete. An energy sword could easily slice through Master Chief’s armor with shields on. However, I would argue that beskar armor isn’t impressive armor tech on Star Wars’ part, but simply an overpowered material. The armor tech itself is quite simple and primitive, just plate armor. If Halo had access to the overpowered material in beskar, the Spartans would become literally invincible, and you can bet Spartans will have full suits of beskar, instead of just like the Mandalorians’, which only cover half of their body. And the power suits won’t weigh down on the wearer, owing to impressive tech with the neurolinks. So, Halo has the better armor tech. Weapons What weapons does Star Wars have? Blasters that shoot plasma? Halo has plasma shooting guns too. And Halo’s projectile-based weapons aren’t shabby either. They probably hurt more than blasters, and they definitely fire much faster with greater range and accuracy. Star Wars has lightsabers? Very cool. But Halo has energy swords too. But Halo also has unique weapons. The needle for example. Does Star Wars have homing bullets? No. Or the Ravager. It might be trash in the actual game, but the tech is great. If any Rebel had a Ravager, they’d be able to charge and fire, and burn through whole squads of stormtroopers. SPNKR will spank your ass, even if you’re a battle tank. Star Wars rocket launchers cannot compete. Cindershot’s huge streaks of bouncing death? Again, if a Rebel had a Cindershot, they can clear our a whole corridor in a second with ease. Halo weaponry tech wins by a huge margin. The fact that Halo armor exists within a universe with this kind of weaponry also makes me appreciate the armor even more. If Star Wars armor pales in comparison, even when they’re up against less lethal weaponry, then Halo armor tech is all the more impressive in comparison. I really wanted Star Wars to win, but unfortunately, Halo technology wins by a landslide. In both categories. (I can, however, take comfort in the knowledge that Star Wars ships in space would beat the crap out of Halo ships.)

Question: Was Palpatine able to teach Anakin/Darth Vader how to be bad and mean?
Answer: Palpatine didn’t have to teach that. Anakin, like most people, naturally has desires and negative emotions. It could be greed for money and power, want of control, anger, jealousy, gluttony, etc. We might give in to these impulses and do morally questionable things, or we might resist our desires and still follow what is right and just. That is basically what Jedi are trying to do with part of their training, to suppress or even root out such negative emotions and impulses. Only, they hold themselves to much higher standards. Plus, being able to connect with the Force grants them great power, and to borrow from a certain Uncle Ben, “With great power comes great responsibility.” The training to fortify the mind and to become paragons of virtue is to be responsible with the power that the Force provides. Palpatine never needed to teach Anakin/Vader to be bad and mean, because the badness and meanness were always there. All Palpatine needed to do was to take advantage of Anakin’s vulnerabilities. The cracks in Anakin’s mind’s fortress that he hasn’t finished training to fully mature and solidify. With the right circumstances, these cracks burst forth and the whole fortress comes tumbling down. Once Anakin stops acting like a Jedi and suppressing his immoral and negative impulses, he acts on his impulses to satisfy his desires. He acts irrationally, and in a bad and mean way. And of course, Palpatine and the dark side encourage him to give in to feelings like anger and hatred. To use it. To not hold back and let “weakness” take over. And if you have ever gotten worked up over something, like an unfair accusation, a partner cheating, or even just a traffic jam, you’ll know that negativity often goes in a vicious cycle. One bad thought leads to another, and more negativity brews, and soon you might be in an uncontrollable rage. You might have been bad and mean. If we all could use the Force, road rage will have much more dire consequences, I’m sure. Vader is simply in such a vicious cycle, and never got out, as the dark side and his own condition simply drag him down, deeper and deeper. He becomes broken. Negativity becomes the only thing he knows how to do, and the dark side and all that has happened seem to give him justification to do it more, and he never escapes the clutches. All Palpatine has to do is lay back and watch.

Question: If you and Kathy Griffin were the last 2 people on the planet, would you be able to reproduce with her or would you let humanity come to an end?
Answer: Humanity will come to an end regardless of what we do. First things first, I doubt she is able to reproduce at her age. And even if she is, and we are both willing, humanity still has no hope whatsoever. If there are only two individuals in an animal species left, then that species will go extinct. Ever heard of inbreeding? Yeah. If we reproduce, then our offspring will have similar genes. And then they reproduce with the same genes. There would simply not be enough variation in the genes to sustain the species, and we would die out. Stemming from this, there is a concept called minimum viable population size in biology. It denotes the minimum number of individuals in the population required for a high probability of the survival of the population. The minimum viable population size for humans would be in the hundreds to the thousands. If there are only 2 people left, humanity has a 0% chance of survival. Heck, let alone2, even if there are 20 fertile people left, there still aren’t very good odds.

Question: Is the Jedi mind trick a stronger form of mind control, than the Kaminoan inhibitor chips or the Geonosian parasites?
Answer: To compare how strong they are, I think we can look at how someone can resist them. For a Kaminoan inhibitor chip, the only way seems to be to remove them. No clone with a functioning chip was able to resist its effects, not even Rex. For a Geonoisan worm, the only way seems to be to not come into contact with them. No clone or Jedi seems to be able to resist. In other words, for the Kamionaon inhibitor chips and Geonoisan parasites, there is no way to resist their mind control. The only way to avoid being mind controlled is to avoid these things altogether. Now, what about the Jedi mind trick? The Jedi mind trick is useless against some species. Even for species that aren’t immune to the trick, all it takes to resist mind control is… a strong mind. That’s it. That’s like having handcuffs that can restrain someone… unless they are strong. Thus, I don’t think the Jedi mind trick can even qualify as mind control. It’s merely a very strong form of persuasion, that works almost as well as mind control on weak minds. The other two solidly qualify, however, and they are undoubtedly stronger, as you can’t resist control simply by having a strong mind.

Question: What if people became immortal and stopped aging at say 25 but also couldn't have babies anymore?
Answer: It would be the greatest thing to ever happen to humanity since our existence. So much of the potential of humans is “wasted” on: Think about it. Name: Arthur Huan
Question: What chess openings have never been defeated?
Answer: I was going to say none. In chess, even the best openings don’t give you a 100% win rate. And enough people have played it that even the most niche openings have been played enough times that someone must have lost with every opening. Even the biggest lead can be blundered. Or perhaps the player resigned due to family emergencies. As long as an opening can be beaten, it has been beaten before. An iteration of Murphy’s law, I guess. Unless an opening somehow makes the other side have insufficient material, it can be beaten. Of course, if you take that many pieces, that won’t count as an opening by then. Wait. I know! Now I do realize there are a few openings that have been defeated. For example, a variation of the King’s Pawn opening, following 1. e4 e5 If the players play 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 Nf6 4. Qxf7#, it’s an unbeaten chess opening called Scholar’s Mate. The opening is never beaten, because it ends in checkmate. Similarly, there’s the even simpler, and even rarer, Fool’s Mate. These are the only kind of openings that have never been beaten. Openings that end with one side winning.

Question: If Darth Vader was the vice president of the entire Galaxy for about 20 years why couldn't he find beskar and make his suit out of that considering this alloy can deflect Blaster shots and is resistant to lightsaber cuts?

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Does Darth Vader overestimate his own power?
Answer: He does not. Vader certainly doesn’t overestimate his own power. He is indeed the most powerful Force user in the galaxy, rivaled only by Yoda and Sidious. What he does overestimate, however, is his judgment. It’s perhaps also accurate to say that he underestimates his opponents. And I know you asked about Vader and not Anakin, but I just cannot help but mention when Anakin first encountered Dooku. It’s a perfect example of what I’m saying. Anakin is not overestimating his power here. He has a pretty good understanding of it, in that he is one of the Jedi Order’s most powerful Jedi in combat. But he did underestimate Dooku. He didn’t think for a moment that perhaps Dooku could be so powerful that he would not be able to contend with Dooku. And I could see why he would make that mistake. He would not have been defeated so quickly even against Windu or Yoda, so it’s natural that he thinks he would at least have a shot against anyone. He also overestimated his own judgment, in that he thought he was right and Obi-Wan was overly cautious. Of course, Obi-Wan had the better judgment. Anakin wasn’t defeated so quickly because he was not powerful enough, he was defeated because he had poor judgment and rushed in with his body completely exposed. (Yoda or Windu would not have been able to exploit this poor judgment, by the way, Anakin would have had his lightsaber up by the time he got within their lightsaber range.) I hope you see what I mean by saying he underestimates his opponents and overestimates his judgment. The same is accurate for Vader. It’s even clearer in Vader’s case, in fact. Vader was indeed the most powerful man in the entire galaxy, rivaled only by Sidious and Yoda. He didn’t overestimate his power. Whenever someone escapes him or even defeats him, it’s never because he thought of himself as more powerful than he was. It was almost always due to Vader’s poor judgment and some extremely lucky circumstances. And if Anakin’s poor judgment was because he was young and overconfident, Vader’s poor judgment was because he sometimes is consumed by rage and the enjoyment of inflicting pain. Take Rogue One, for example. He was enjoying himself too much in massacring the Rebels, that he lost sight of the main objective. Or in Rebels, when he let Kanan and Ezra get away. He underestimated their resourcefulness and luck (read: plot armor). Or in Fallen Order. He was enjoying himself against Cere and Cal, and he didn’t think of the Empire’s cheap glass and the water outside. Or in the Kenobi show recently. Same thing. He wanted to inflict the most pain, which ultimately gave his prey the chance to evade him. Plus, he was consumed by rage and hatred. Also note that for every lucky protagonist we see, Vader successfully tortured and killed many more. Survivorship bias and/or plot armor are very much present. The bottom line is that Vader was really as good and powerful as he thought he was. He occasionally would underestimate his opponents and the circumstances, but that’s it. (Almost everyone else succumbs to the same issue, by the way, including Sidious, Windu, and Yoda. Nobody is omniscient, apparently.)

Question: What would happen if a Jedi use the lightsaber to slash a droideka with shield still on? Never seen that in Star Wars, want to know if they're lightsaber proof

Question: Why do people think Windu would have lost to Dooku when he quite easily defeated Sidious?
Answer: I do not know. Perhaps they were looking at a younger version of both Dooku and Windu. Before Dooku left the Jedi Order, he was the best duelist, second only to Yoda. This means at that time, he was superior to Windu. But of course, at this time the two wouldn’t get into a real fight. A fight between the two would be very volatile and there is no clear winner. Windu is more favored, but there is no guarantee. Just like there was no guarantee that Windu could have beaten Sidious.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Are Ahsoka and Luke equally skilled, knowledgeable, and powerful in the ways of the force?
Answer: No. Two people are very rarely equal on anything, let alone when you compare three metrics. It also depends a lot on the when. For example, Ahsoka was already a powerful Force user when Luke was stumbling around on Tatooine. And Ahsoka might’ve already died by the Sequels when Luke was former Grandmaster of the Order. For a fair comparison, I’ll pick The Mandalorian as the point in time to compare the two. They’re arguably close to their primes, and both have had opportunities to learn and grow sufficiently, with neither going into recline yet. Skills: Ahsoka wins Ahsoka was trained in the Jedi Order, with many Jedi around. She had all the necessary resources. She underwent systematic and rigorous training for years, under mentors like Yoda and Plo Koon. After this, she trained under and fought with Anakin. She was taught by some of the greatest Jedi, and her skills were properly taught and refined. Luke, on the other hand, didn’t have the same resources. He managed to learn a lot from Yoda and Obi-Wan, and from Force ghosts and Jedi texts. But, ultimately, it’s very different from being trained by a living Jedi who can spar with you and offer constant, real-time instruction. Plus, Ahsoka’s experience and extra time in real situations don’t hurt either. Therefore, Ahsoka is more skilled. Knowledge: Ahsoka Just like skill, Ahsoka benefits from having spent her teenage years as a part of the Jedi Order. She had access to Jedi Masters, a library, and all the other facilities in the Temple. She had war experience. She had mentors and teachers. And of course, she has had almost two decades on Luke. Luke has certainly learned a lot, and he learns knowledge about the Force easier than most, courtesy of his high Force potential. However, the gap is still there. This doesn’t take away from Luke in any way, as Ahsoka had long since been a seasoned veteran/mentor figure for younger Jedi. This includes Luke. She is the new Yoda of sorts. Give Luke a few decades of his own, and the new grandmaster could well have more knowledge than Ahsoka at that point. But not now. Power: Luke Luke is a Skywalker, and his potential is much higher than Ahsoka’s. Apart from his father, and perhaps his sister Leia, nobody rivals his Force potential. Provided that he came close to realizing his potential, his connection to the Force is much stronger than Ahsoka’s, and he’s more powerful. Of course, power alone is not enough to determine a fight, the individuals also matter. See the fight between Anakin and Obi-Wan, the fight between Vader and Obi-Wan, and the fight between Vader and Obi-Wan. “Ahsoka, learn from me, they love me.” or something like that Therefore, as Ahsoka is much more experienced and skilled, if she fought Luke, she still might be able to win.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Why did the Jedi think adults were too old to be taught the ways of the force, even though the Sith managed it just fine?
Answer: It wasn’t about learning the ways of the Force. It was about learning the ways of the Jedi. Jedi are more than Force users. More importantly, Jedi are warrior monks. They are akin to Shaolin monks, among others. Central to the Jedi philosophy, is the mindset and lifestyle. These things take precedence over knowledge or combat skills. You have to be a Jedi before you can be a good Jedi. And just like real-world religions, it’s better to start young. Most people got their religion from their parents, as they grew up submerged in the religion. Real-world monks can often start late, but undoubtedly the ones that start young generally have an easier time. And we might only notice lightsaber training for younglings. This is important, as learning any skill is easier when young. But also notice that here, they are actually also being taught to sense the Force and feel their relation to it, as well as monitor their feelings and awareness. Plus, for our monks, the stakes are lower. If a Buddhist monk fails to reach enlightenment, that’s fine. It’ll still be a moral and meaningful life for him. If a Christian monk goes back on the conversion of life, they might be condemned by the religious figures, but they wouldn’t be committing crimes. With these monks, you’ll just revert back to being an ordinary person. You don’t just become a danger to society. But if Jedi do not train their minds properly, they might fall to the dark side. They don’t just become ordinary people, no. They could become evil. And with great ability comes great ability to do evil. With such a danger on the horizon, it’s imperative to gain the advantages that can be gained. In conclusion, Jedi training starts early, because training the mind is the most important part of being a Jedi, and starting young makes it much easier — necessary, even — for most people who aren’t prodigies. With Sith, it doesn’t matter so much. They usually give in to their emotions and impulses that Jedi train for decades to get rid of or control. Sith still do need training with their mindset and how they handle their emotions, but it’s far less demanding.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: Why do people scream when they get cut with a lightsaber?
Answer: Because when you get cut, you feel immense pain. When you feel immense pain, you scream. So what is pain? Unfortunately, I cannot explain it. It’s an instance of “qualia”. It’s a purely subjective experience that only exists in our minds. And just as it’s impossible to explain color to a blind person who has never seen color, it is also impossible to convey what pain is, to someone who has never felt pain. But to get back to the question, almost all people do feel pain. When our body is damaged, like when burnt, electrocuted, or cut, we will feel a very bad feeling called pain. And if that pain is intense, people will scream. That’s why people scream when they get cut with a lightsaber.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: If Darth Vader had a chance to start over as Anakin, would he?
Answer: No, but yes. Darth Vader is undeniably proud that he destroyed Anakin, and he sees himself as stronger than Anakin. It’s fair to say that part of his core identity is that he is the one who destroyed the weak Anakin. “Anakin was weak. I destroyed him.” As well as countless other instances. Vader saw Anakin as weak, and he has now risen above, embracing the dark side, and gained everything he ever wanted. He has the power he craves. So why would he want to go back to being Anakin? He won’t. I can stop here, but I’m not going to. Just like Luke, I want to go further and see what’s inside. This is not who Vader is. Let’s start with the obvious. Vader did not destroy Anakin. There is still Anakin within him. And Anakin keeps coming back, when he met Ahsoka, when he met Obi-Wan, and when he met his son. Vader keeps trying to lock that part of him away, but he cannot. This doesn’t mean Vader would want to be Anakin again, but it does tell us that he is in conflict. The dark side usually wins these conflicts massively, almost making it seem as if there isn’t anything else. However, there always is. And the reason that the dark side wins is that Vader is broken and trapped. He’s trapped in the swamps of his mental baggage. He never pulled himself out of the swamp, because it was simply too difficult. He was too broken and the dark side’s grasp too great. However, if you can teleport him out, revert all the brokenness, and give him back Padme and everything else, he will take it. That won’t be difficult. That bypasses everything and lets him avoid all responsibility. So long as he doesn’t have to work and face things himself, he will want to revert things. EDIT: Plus, he would get Padme back. In RotJ, he turned back to Anakin just out of love for Luke. He didn’t even think he’d have a life with his children after the act. Now if you just let him start over as Anakin, he’d even be able to lead a life with Padme. I don’t think it’ll be an offer that Vader can turn down.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: What colour crystal do you think Cal Kestis would canonically have and why?
Answer: It’s not a matter for me to express my opinion. Cal Kestis is canon, the game is canon, and he has an official lightsaber color. As the game is canon, his original lightsaber color is blue. And then he could possibly have any of the other five colors too. This is the problem with games like this, where you have a choice in the story. It makes the canon confusing. Are all the storylines with the different choices canon? Or just one of them? Which one? And why? It’s less of an issue when the difference is arbitrary, like an option to say “Hello” instead of “Hey, what’s up?”, but more problematic for things that matter more. In this case, the issue is bypassed, as it’s just arbitrarily set that the lightsaber color stayed blue as canon. Both of Cal Kestis’s lightsabers canonically are blue. As for why, there isn’t a why. Otherwise, Jedi get blue or green kyber crystals, and it’s either up to their favorite color or by random. In canon, unlike Legends, the lightsaber color isn’t correlated to the wielder. NOTE: [LEGENDS CONTENT] If we consider the warrior/guardian/sentinel thing in Legends, then I’d argue Cal Kestis is a sentinel. He is balanced in his approach to both combat skills and knowledge about the Force, and he rounds out his inventory with non-Force skills. Then, it’d be fitting if his blade is yellow or orange.

Name: Arthur Huan
Question: What happens if you break your lightsaber blade?
Answer: You cannot. It’s like asking “What happens if you break the stream of water from your tap?” Lightsabers blades aren’t solid, so you cannot break their blade. They are made of plasma, a subset of gasses. And if you cannot break the air around you by waving your hand, you cannot break the plasma blade of a lightsaber. What you can do is break the lightsaber hilt itself, and then you’d just have a non-functional lightsaber. NOTE: If you are talking about the “lightsabers” we can buy, they’re just LED tubes. So you’ll just end up with a broken tube. Nothing extraordinary would happen.

Question: Would Emperor Palpatine, Darth Vader, and the Imperial Inquisitors have been able to defeat Abeloth if she emerged and attacked the Galactic Empire?
Answer: Probably yes. Though the Inquisitors wouldn’t contribute much. [LEGENDS CONTENT] Abeloth was “killed” by Luke and Darth Krayt. Question: If he had stayed with the Empire, would Han Solo have been a good officer?
Answer: No, unless this is what you think a good officer is: Han wanted to be a TIE Fighter pilot, but he ended up as a mudtrooper: Let’s see what this means. Mudtroopers are part of the Imperial Army. The Imperial Army, just like real-life armies, has commissioned officers and enlisted personnel. Commissioned officers go through officer school, and if they graduate, they become officers. Enlisted personnel, on the other hand, are enlisted as regular soldiers, though they can rise in rank and eventually become non-commissioned officers. However, non-commissioned officers are still subordinate to commissioned officers. So even if Han is the greatest soldier ever, the highest rank he can achieve will still be insignificant compared to the hierarchy. What’s worse, he’s a mudtrooper. Not a stormtrooper. The Stormtrooper Corps is an elite branch of the Imperial Army. A stormtrooper private would likely be held in greater regard than a mudtrooper sergeant. So Han is not in a great position to be a good officer. It’s quite literally not possible. He didn’t go through officer school, or stormtrooper academy, so the best he can be is a low-ranked officer that will eventually die on the worst battlefields possible. Furthermore, he’s not the kind of person who could be a good officer. Han is not loyal to the Empire, and has no respect for authority. He has no discipline. He is not motivated to perform well for the Empire. There’s no way he will rise through the ranks to even become a good mudtrooper officer. EDIT: I just realized that Han is actually not a mudtrooper. He is still an Imperial Naval cadet. Infantry duty as a mudtrooper is a punishment for disobedient cadets. This makes the previous point about mudtroopers being lower than stormtroopers irrelevant. Being part of the Imperial Navy, he won’t face that discrimination due to an elite branch, so he could be a great non-commissioned officer if he puts his mind to it. No serious mortality either. Truly a math problem completely detached from reality. With this, we just have to determine the population for each generation. We can notice that every 2 people produces 4 people, so it’s simply the population doubling every generation. Let the generation number be x. Then: So we would cross 8 billion after generation 33. Question: Why is there a 50-move rule and a 75-move rule?
Answer: Imagine I am playing chess with you in a tournament, and we both have an hour left on the clock with the following position: What happens? As White, I am an entire rook up in material, and if you mess up one move, I have Qxb8# checkmate. But Black’s saving grace is that White had completely neglected king safety. And so Black could avoid certain loss by perpetually checking White. As White, I would never agree to a draw because you cannot checkmate me easily unless I blunder terribly, but if I somehow get out of the perpetual check, I would be completely winning. As Black, you cannot force a draw by three-fold repetition either. What happens? You just have to keep checking me repeatedly, and I have to keep moving my king. The game cannot end until someone makes a mistake, or until the time runs out. Realizing this, both of us start to blitz out our moves. Whoever can run down the opponent’s time first would win. And remember, we both have 1 hour on our clock. Imagine playing bullet chess for 1 hour without stopping. It wouldn’t be a game of chess anymore, it would be a game of hand endurance. Though useful for determining who is more pathetic in their love life, it’s not chess anymore. Therefore, the 50 move limit is set, so that you can claim a draw after 50 moves. This way, you cannot perpetually prolong the game. And if for some reason both players want to continue, a 75-move rule would force a draw even if neither player claims the draw. Here’s just an example of a series of 50 moves: 1.Kg3 Qg6+ 2.Kf2 Qf5+ 3.Kg3 Qg6+ 4.Kf2 Qf5+ 5.Ke2 Qh5+ 6.Ke3 Qh3+ 7.Ke2 Qh5+ 8.Ke1 Qh1+ 9.Ke2 Qg2+ ( 9...Qh2+ ) 10.Kd3 Qg6+ 11.Ke2 Qg2+ 12.Kd3 Qg6+ 13.Ke3 Qg1+ 14.Ke2 Qg4+ 15.Ke3 Qg1+ 16.Ke2 Qg4+ 17.Kd2 Qg5+ 18.Kd3 Qf5+ 19.Ke3 Qh3+ 20.Kd2 Qg2+ 21.Ke3 Qg3+ 22.Ke2 Qg2+ 23.Kd1 Qg4+ 24.Kd2 Qf4+ 25.Ke2 Qg4+ 26.Kd3 Qf5+ 27.Ke3 Qh3+ 28.Kd2 Qh6+ 29.Kd3 Qg6+ 30.Kd2 Qg5+ 31.Ke1 Qh4+ 32.Kf1 Qh1+ 33.Kf2 Qh2+ 34.Kf1 Qh3+ 35.Ke2 Qg2+ 36.Kd3 Qf1+ 37.Kd2 Qf2+ 38.Kd1 Qf3+ 39.Ke1 Qg3+ 40.Kd1 Qf3+ 41.Ke1 Qe4+ 42.Kd2 Qg2+ 43.Kd3 Qf1+ 44.Ke3 Qh3+ 45.Ke2 Qg2+ 46.Kd3 Qg6+ 47.Ke3 Qg3+ 48.Ke2 Qh2+ 49.Kd3 Qh3+ 50.Ke2 Qg2+ * And it can go on forever. Though, the variation at move 9 is an example of how Black might blunder to lose. It’s not obvious, but after 10. Kd3 Qg3+ 11. Be3, we reach this position: Just like that, I’ve gotten out of the perpetual check, and Black is now doomed. This is, luckily, what happened in my own game and I went on to win as White.

Question: Yoda once said that fear leads to anger, anger leads to hate and hate leads to suffering. The last two make sense, but how would fear lead to anger?
Answer: I think it would be easier to explain with an example, so let’s just start with a hypothetical example. Suppose we have a person, who we'll call A for now. Let’s start with fear. A is fearful of something. Let’s say for example he is fearful of losing loved ones. Fear as an emotion arises when you anticipate danger. A anticipates the possibility of losing loved ones, suppose for example his mother or his wife. He has fear in his heart. (And if, god forbid, the danger is realized, it could serve to intensify fear for other similar dangers. Like if A loses his mother or wife, he’d be more scared of losing the other person too.) And if fear comes out of the anticipation of danger, anger could come out of displeasure and annoyance at not being able to avoid the danger. People like control. When we fear something, and we fear it long enough, we will start to be frustrated and resentful that we don’t have control and we cannot prevent it. In our example, A fears loss, and eventually, he will be distressed that he cannot prevent loss. And it could very likely lead to anger.

Question: Why do people talk as if Star Wars is real and the events and planets are real and happened?
Answer: As the majority of my answers on Quora fit this description, I feel it is appropriate that I address this. Note this isn’t limited to Star Wars, it extends to all works of fiction. Let’s begin with some reasons, shall we? 1 - In-universe consistency Yes, Star Wars is not real, and the rules in the world could be different from ours, but there still needs to be consistency within the fictional universe. If it’s established that a magical mushroom will turn you smaller, then when Alex eats the magical mushroom, she must turn small. If it’s established that a laser destroys planets, that laser cannot then help the planet grow more trees. It doesn't matter how unusual or fantastical a fictional world is, but it matters a whole lot whether or not that world has coherence and consistency within itself. Convincing stories must be in a universe where there is internal logic. And in order to discuss the internal logic, we have to talk about it. And we have to first accept the world-building and the rules of the fictional world. 2 - “Star Wars fans are nerds and nerds have no life.” While the above statement is a clear-cut case of bullying, there is more to it if you stop and think about it. Nerds have a superpower. The superpower to experience other lives in other worlds. As I wrote in a primary school essay, Books are the keys to whole new worlds. When I pick up my Kindle, I can go dueling with Draco Malfoy, or marvel at the magical beasts in Narnia. I can hold my breath with Anne Frank, waiting for the Nazis to pass. I can wallow in misery as I dig holes with Stanley in Holes. Books allow me to explore new worlds. And not only do I enjoy books because of this, but what I experience in the new worlds adds back to my own life in my own world. If you submerge yourself in these new worlds, you’ll know what I was talking about. It’s amazing and wonderful. I pity people who don’t like to read. While Star Wars doesn’t just consist of books, the principle is the same. It’s a great thing to submerge yourself in literary worlds and explore. 3 - It’s fun Seriously. This alone should be enough reason. It’s fun to engage in discourse about Star Wars, pretending it’s real. Or at least temporarily diving into the world and seeing it from the perspective of the characters, for whom the world is indeed real And if you turn up your nose at our ways of having fun because it’s not real… Remember none of these are real either. There is no real benefit to carrying a ball into a zone, kicking a ball into a net, or throwing a ball into a basket. We only agreed to all pretend these are desirable. People pretend something is real for the sake of fun. So when Star Wars fans agree to temporarily pretend the events happened, that’s equally valid, is it not?

Question: Brian Sykes (geneticist) said males "are really not that necessary." Is that true?
Answer: It is technically true. Neither are females. The entire system of sexes and gender is not necessary for life. After all, bacteria and many other microorganisms exist just fine without sexual reproduction. Yeast, which is what makes our bread rise, has no male or female. A yeast would simply “bud” and reproduce on its own. It’s called asexual reproduction, or reproduction that doesn’t require sex. If, however, you have higher aspirations than being one of the millions of microorganisms that are eaten as part of bread each day, you start to need both males and females. While you don’t need sexes for life itself, you do need sexes for complex life. In fact, it’s been theorized that sexual reproduction was a prerequisite for complex life. Regardless, it’s clear to see why sexual reproduction is very advantageous and a requirement for complex life to survive and flourish. In evolution, the variation of traits within a species is paramount. Otherwise, when the environment changes drastically (“when”, not “if”) the whole species might be wiped out. With variation, some members might be able to survive. The species would be able to adapt. Long story short, variation is good. Especially so for complex organisms (who require more energy and are more dependent on their environment, for one). Asexual reproduction doesn't give much variation. With asexual reproduction, the parent simply copies itself to make offspring. Meanwhile, any high schooler can tell you just how amazingly good sexual reproduction is at producing variation. During meiosis, the genes from each parent are randomly selected, and mixed together to form unique, distinct combinations. On top of that, there is crossing over to introduce even more variations. This is one of the important reasons why virtually all complex organisms reproduce sexually. Even if asexual reproduction isn’t problematic for complex organisms, the fact of the matter is, we Homo Sapiens reproduce sexually. That is not going to change. And if you are gonna reproduce sexually, you need both males and females. That’s the whole point. So do we need males and females? Yes. Unless you want to be a significantly simpler form of life.
