Question: Do some chess players try to exchange pieces and simplify things when playing against a much stronger opponent? Is it advisable to do so?
Answer: Yes, many chess players try to exchange pieces and simplify things, especially lower-rated players. It is not advisable to do so. Don’t get me wrong, I’m not saying it’s a bad idea to trade. There are many scenarios where it is a great idea to trade. I am only saying that: Trading material for the sake of “simplifying” is not a great idea. It’s the wrong reason. Because guess what? When you “simplify” the board, it will end up being more complicated. Take this position for example: Seems rather simple, right? Half of the pieces from both sides are gone. This position is actually from the FIDE Candidates tournament, the tournament between the world’s greatest chess players to determine who will challenge the world champion for that title. The game is from a Round 1 game between Hikaru Nakamura and Fabiano Caruana. Both are super GMs, near the current peak of the human mind in chess. Yet, in this “simple” position, both made a string of “mistakes” and “blunders” according to the computer engines. Meanwhile, in a more “complicated” position: Round 5 game between Hikaru and Nepo The players were able to play a continuous string of near-perfect moves. Not only that, but it took them much less thinking and time to find the best moves. How? As it turns out, in chess, often the simpler a position is, the more complex and difficult evaluation of it is. When there are more pieces on the board, there are more pieces that you have to watch, but most of these pieces aren’t actually doing much at a time. The extra pieces restrict the movement and positioning of some of the more active pieces. By having fewer pieces, it often is a more open board, meaning more freedom and more calculations required. Therefore, exchanging material merely for the sake of simplifying is often counterproductive. It ends up making the future harder to see as all the pieces now have more variations. Of course, it still always depends on the situation. For example: White to move. If white trades rooks, then the game becomes simple and there is no chance for black anymore. The remaining white rook will ensure the black king cannot reach any action, and the white pawn will promote faster. In this case, the position does become simpler, and even if white is trading a queen for a rook, it’s arguably a worthwhile endeavor to make the win more assured. Trades are also often worthwhile to improve the position. The most common trade I do in my own playing is this one: As Black, I always trade bishops. It leads to the best position for me. As I said previously, trading isn’t a bad idea, as long as you do it for the right reasons. The only problem is if you trade merely because you want to think about fewer pieces, believing it will simplify the position. It usually doesn’t. Trade pieces for the right reasons.

Question: Is it a sign of disrespect that the other Inquisitors consistently refer to Reva by her first name instead of "Third Sister"?

It seems they are still individuals with individuality. In this light, the focus is on the person having a new identity. And Third Sister doesn’t want her old identity. She considers her old identity weak, her old identity has too much pain, and the other Inquisitors constantly berate her for her past. As the Grand Inquisitor said, she was a rat in the sewers, before they found her and took her in. They think of her as lowly and filthy underneath. Question: Why do Star Wars fans dislike Reva so much?
Answer: I’d like to reiterate that we need to keep in mind the loud minority can often skew our perception. Furthermore, just because there are some racist comments, doesn’t mean all criticism of the character is racist hate. With that out of the way, here’s some criticism of the character. [SPOILER-FREE] #1 - Lack of backstory And the sad thing is, the show genuinely tried to give her a backstory and motivation with an early scene in Episode I and a monologue to the little girl prisoner in Episode IV. However, it’s still not easy to see where she’s coming from, both literally and metaphorically. Like why the obsession? She is more obsessed than the people who should actually care, like Vader. Somehow, I feel Reva had about as much backstory as Cara Dune. What is different is that Cara was a side character. Even if she wasn’t in The Mandalorian, nothing would’ve needed to change. Meanwhile, Reva is supposed to be the main antagonist. With your main villain, especially one that has sidelined Vader in a show about Vader’s former master, there are much higher expectations the character must meet. #2 - She “usurped” Obi-Wan and Vader The show is called Obi-Wan Kenobi. So he is the protagonist. Who is the antagonist? For the longest time, fans believed it would be Vader. Of course, there’d be a few Inquisitors, but Vader is the ultimate boss. He has the deepest personal connection with Kenobi, plus he is the one who has the skills to actually contend with Kenobi. On top of that, Hayden Christensen being confirmed to play Vader created a huge buzz. And then, Vader was put into the background. Even Obi-Wan was not as clear as the main character. Reva became the pseudo-protagonist of the show. This certainly would be very upsetting for many fans. #3 - She is comically evil and unlikeable Somehow, Reva is just as evil and brutal as Vader, and even more unlikeable. The Grand Inquisitor and the Fifth Brother turned into relatively good guys compared to her. That’s right. She makes the Grand Inquisitor seem like a likable good guy. There is, of course, a way to make a purely evil character work. Palpatine worked. But they didn’t make Reva work. #4 - Lack of diversity of facial expression This picture is about the only face of Reva you’ll see. I don’t know if the writers wrote it like that, the director told her to be like that, or if the actress is like this. I’ve certainly seen a lot better facial expressions from Moses Ingram in Queen’s Gambit. #5 - She is no Vader or Fett Or Mando. They have the cool factor. Reva’s coolness isn’t enough to make her loved though. EDIT: [SPOILER ALERT FOR EPISODE 5] Seriously, huge spoiler alert. Even if you’re okay with normal spoilers, I’d highly recommend turning back here. When Reva talks to Obi-Wan through the doorway, I think her backstory is finally fleshed out to an acceptable degree. So let’s go through my points again. #1 - Lack of backstory Changed to “confusing backstory”. Reva was was one of the younglings during Order 66 and saw her teachers slaughtered by clones. Then Anakin came to “help”. She survived by pretending to be dead, but obviously it was a traumatic event. Eventually, she becomes an Inquisitor. She swears to extract revenge by killing Vader. Okay. Then why did she go after Jedi so much? I can understand if she is actually turned to the dark side and is now working for Vader, and wants to impress him by being brutal to Jedi and perhaps eventually catching Kenobi. But if her end goal is to kill Vader, none of what she does helps that goal. It’s not like only the Grand Inquisitor can meet Vader and it’s not like she hasn’t met Vader in all sorts of situations before. #2 - She “usurped” Obi-Wan and Vader Yes. Even in an espisode where the entire situation is mapped to a prior duel between Obi-Wan and Anakin, it’s still not about Obi-Wan or Vader. Reva is still the main character. #3 - She is comically evil and unlikeable Even more so, though it’s now chaotic and messy. Just like #1, it’s confusing. Does she want to kill Vader? Does she want to be the best Inquisitor possible? Or is she so absolutely retarded that she actually dreams of perhaps replacing Vader under Sidious? That’s the only explanation I can come up with for how she acts. But I don’t think she is mentally disabled, she is shown as a rather smart and calculating character, so… Why? #4 - Lack of diversity of facial expression Yep. Though it might be excused by the trauma she suffered and the life she lead. It’s useful to have a poker face and it’s reasonable that she’s always mad, vengeful, and unhinged. #5 - She is no Vader or Fett No character design changes. So overall, I think all of my 5 points still stand. I won’t be doing a reevaulation when Episode 6 comes out, as that is the final episode. If we need to wait until the last episode to fix the character, it’s a massive failure. Imagine if Ahsoka is an insufferable brat up until Order 66. Nobody would like her, or the Clone Wars show for that matter.

Question: Can I play chess if im not gambling?
Answer: Unless you are betting on the winner, it is not gambling. Even if you do bet on the winner, it is still not gambling. Gambling has to involve betting money on a game of chance. Sure, it often involves skill and a grasp of game theory. Sure, you can count cards in blackjack. However, at the end of the day, these are still games of chance. You can only better manipulate the chances to be in your favor. Chess, on the other hand, is a game of 100% skill. There are no hidden pieces on the opponents’ side that you have to guess. There are no dice dictating any moves. You have all the information and you control everything that happens on the board. Thus, it is not gambling. Chess is a game of skill, not a game of chance. Of course, more importantly than that is whether you can control yourself properly. If you cannot help but bet thousands of dollars on chess games without any self-restraint, resulting in bankruptcy, that is still bad. But you can do that with any game, right? Just be the 99.9% of chess players who don’t bet money.

Question: What Jedi had a unique lightsaber style?
Answer: Jedi Master Depa Billaba. She was trained by this motherfucker: … and she had a unique lightsaber style in Vaapad. Now you might have some questions, ranging from “What is Vaapad?” to “Since when was Vaapad unique?” What is Vaapad? Very quickly, Vaapad is a modified version of Form VII, Juyo. It is the most aggressive of the seven lightsaber styles and highly unpredictable. The most notable practitioner of Vaapad is Mace Windu. Depa Billaba was also able to learn it from her master and mastered it to a very high degree. Since when was Vaapad unique? Since this moment: Vaapad was actually not a very niche lightsaber style. The Jedi Order did frown upon Form VII, and then most people were only able to learn the Juyo variant if they wanted to, but still, it’s a very well-established form. As rare as it might be, there’d still be a lot of practitioners of Vaapad, right? Wrong. Well, maybe technically right. I’m sure there are some Jedi who learned Vaapad and use it. However, they likely aren’t actually using Vaapad. Vaapad is not just a lightsaber style, it is also a mindset. A practitioner of Vaapad channels their inner darkness into the lightsaber duel. This is already hard enough, and if you get it wrong, you might turn to the dark side. In Legends, the Jedi Master who created Vaapad with Windu, himself fell to the dark side. If you can avoid that danger, there is still another challenge. A true master of Vaapad must also be able to channel the opponent’s darkness. This is partly why Windu was able to defeat Sidious: Windu directed Sidious’s dark side back at him. This would be almost impossible. There were only two Jedi in the entire Order who was able to achieve this — Mace Windu and Depa Billaba. They are unique, in that they are able to use true Vaapad and channel the darkness in both themselves and their opponent. Nobody else can do this, thus nobody else actually uses the Vaapad lightsaber style. When Windu died, Depa Billaba became the only Jedi with this lightsaber style. Briefly. She died in Order 66 very soon, but in that short span of time she “had a unique lightsaber style”.

Question: In chess why is the dominant piece called queen and not king? Aren't kings more powerful historically?
Answer: Outside of movies like the Lord of the Rings, where the king is actually a powerful warrior, most historic kings specialize in leadership, not swordsmanship. A king’s power is from his ability to command followers and importance to the sovereignty of a nation. He is, first and foremost, a leader. Not the best fighter. The king in chess is the most important piece, as all pieces must work to protect him. He rallies the troop and the entire army would collapse if he falls. He himself is not the most powerful warrior. Though, I would like to point out that the king is already much more powerful than a pawn, the common soldier. In many circumstances, he is as good as a knight, like in endgames where there are only minor pieces. A knight. A king is often as good as a knight. So we should already applaud him for his combat prowess. There are very few kings who can fight as well as their knights. He is already a great warrior king. On the other hand, the queen in chess is just an unparalleled legend, able to match three ordinary knights combined. Seems the king in chess just found the most badass woman in existence and married her. EDIT: Historical context. The queen wasn’t originally the queen. The piece was called wazeer/wazir, vizir, and ferz in earlier forms (some came earlier than others, of course). Many of the variants moved like the modern chess king, one square in any direction. Later, the piece became widely called the “queen” in the European game that would become chess. She moved one square only. Sometime after that, the powerful moves for the queen and bishop were developed. The pawn’s first double move was also conceived around that rough period. I would argue this was when the game could start to be regarded as the game of chess. I knew this historical context to a basic degree, and I appreciate the more knowledgeable people pointing this out. I didn’t touch on it, though, as I simply didn’t see this angle of approach as the most appealing. Thanks for expanding on the knowledge. What I don’t quite take a liking to is people saying this is the ONLY explanation and any other, like my original one, is incorrect. There are many angles of approach.

Question: Why are chess pieces given different points when only the game matters? Or do the points matter in some cases? If yes, then can you explain those cases?
Answer: Yes, only the game matters. Which is why, I can have a game like this: I am 7 points up as White, I have an extra rook and two pawns, but I still lost because the opponent managed to checkmate me. So I lost. It doesn’t matter if I am 30 points higher than the opponent, if you get checkmate, you lose. However, points are a way to keep track of the relative strength of pieces you have on the board. They are useful, for instance, here: White to move. What should White do? Should White play Nxg6 or Nxd7? How do you determine it based on “the game”? It’s impossible to tell. However, you can look at the points of each play. If you take the bishop, it’s just free 3 points. If you take the rook, they will take it back and it’s only a 2-point advantage (5 minus 3). So then you play Nxg6. And if you are a supercomputer like Stockfish who can also incorporate the positions and game state into the points, you can see that Nxg6 results in about +2.58 advantage, and Nxd7 gives +1.77 advantage. (Stockfish 15, depth 20) Of course, if White blunders, and plays this after taking the bishop: That 3-point material advantage was thrown away. Black can now checkmate and White has lost. But what the points do tell is that relatively speaking, before this blunder, White was stronger by 3 points of material advantage.

Question: Is Liam Neeson going to reprise his role as Qui-Gon in the Kenobi series?
Answer: As of now, I don’t think there is an official confirmation from Liam Neeson or the production crew. But we can speculate to a degree of certainty. [VERY SLIGHT SPOILERS ALERT] At the start of the Kenobi show, there was a recap of past events. From him and Qui-Gon stumbling upon the young Anakin, to training him, to their final fight on Mustafar. But at the end of this recap, there was just one addition that was slipped in. Yoda starts out by telling Obi-Wan “the boy you trained, gone he is” and all the stuff we are familiar with, but he ends by telling Obi-Wan that he has extra training to do, to communicate with his old master. This extra detail jumped out at me, because it was the only part of the recap I was not already familiar with, so they added it for the sake of this show. Foreshadowing #1. Later on, in the same Episode, Obi-Wan had a nightmare. He is startled awake, sits up, and reaches out, asking for guidance from his master.For a moment, I was holding my breath anticipating, but nothing happened. However, they did remind us again of this side storyline that is there. They hinted at it at the very start, during the recap, and are reminding us again. Foreshadowing #2. I think there was also a bit of foreshadowing of this in Episode II, but my memory does not serve me well. What this foreshadowing in the opening episodes of the show does is it seems to set up an inevitable return of Qui-Gon. He is dead, but can still appear in a flashback. More likely than not, he will appear in the show as a Force ghost. By “appear” I don’t mean actually appear, as Qui-Gon didn’t master the technique well enough to be corporeal under normal circumstances. But he can appear as a voice to Obi-Wan. (Thus, hiring Liam Neeson for the voice.) This is not only foreshadowed by the easter eggs, but it’s also a natural thing. Obi-Wan faces a challenging emotional and mental hurdle, which he has apparently failed to get over for the last ten years. This mission off of Tatooine is a massive change in lifestyle, and as he is forced into dilemmas he will be forced to change how he thinks. Perhaps he will figure things out and come out of the gloom that shrouds him. However, it is also mentally challenging and stressful for him. And it’s not hard to get over such regret, guilt, and pain. The guidance and help from a wise mentor is the natural thing for him and for the show. With that said, our expectations could also be subverted. Maybe Neeson would not be in the show. The easter eggs and predictions above are shared by many. And there are plenty of people like me, ready to point it out to everyone and explain exactly why Qui-Gon will be in the show. That could be exactly why Qui-Gon will not be in the show. Obi-Wan very well could get over it on his own. Or perhaps with the help of Leia. She might not be a wise old mentor, but her connection to Anakin, as well as her traits, might spark some things for Obi-Wan. As likely as it would be for Qui-Gon to talk to him and help him, it’s also very possible that Obi-Wan will recover without the help. He’ll come to terms with what happened, and let the future happen. He’ll patiently wait and learn to let go. Soon enough he will become a Force ghost as well, hopefully after the Empire is vanquished. Maybe he will speak to his master then. EDIT: The part of the recap I thought was added on was actually in the original Revenge of the Sith movie. An old friend has learned the path to immortality. One who has returned from the netherworld of the force, your old master. Thanks to Jake for pointing it out to me. I had completely forgotten this was there. Regardless, the all-important opening recap ending with this line and reminding us is still of importance.

Question: In the Star Wars show Obi-Wan, Vader is commanding a small army of Sith (or renegade Jedi, same diff) warriors. Is this a problem for the emperor?
Answer: “Vader is commanding a small army of Sith (or renegade Jedi, same diff) warriors.” The problem is that it is NOT “same diff”. The difference is instead of vital importance. The Inquisitors are not Sith, and they don’t aspire to be unless they are very stupid. Additionally, Vader does not command them. Let’s start with the important distinction between Sith and the Inquisitors. The Inquisitors are simply dark side Force users that work for Sidious and Vader. They are not Sith, because Sith is a special ideology, and Sith Lord is a special title. Only Vader and Sidious are Sith during the Empire times. The second point is that the Inquisitors do not answer to Vader. They answer to Sidious. Sidious created the Inquisitorius in the first place, and they are to serve him. They do often follow Vader, as normally he is representing the Emperor. He can also step in and lead them for Sidious, usually for tougher cases, like Eath Koth, or Kenobi right now. However, fundamentally, they follow the authority of Sidious. Vader only leads them because Sidious told them to follow. If Sidious takes back the authority that he “lent” to Vader, the Inquisitors would not listen to Vader anymore.
